title: Hands-On Data Analysis Using Jamovi
text:
Preface
Statistical analysis begins with a research question and ends with a statement that another reader can evaluate. Between these points, the researcher must define the population, understand how observations were collected, choose an appropriate summary or model, examine assumptions, and explain uncertainty. Software supports these decisions; it does not make them on the researcher’s behalf.
This book is written for medical students, clinicians, postgraduate trainees, and health researchers beginning applied data analysis. Its purpose is to connect a clinical question with the structure of the data, the statistical method, and the meaning of the result. The emphasis is on estimates and their uncertainty, supported by appropriate tests and clear reporting. The American Statistical Association’s statement provides the basis for interpreting a p-value in context rather than treating a threshold as a complete scientific conclusion. [1]

title: Hands-On Data Analysis Using Jamovi
text:
What this volume covers
Volume I covers the foundations needed to analyse a straightforward health dataset: study design, variable types, data entry and validation, cleaning and missing values, transformations, preparation for a specific analysis, descriptive statistics, graphs, uncertainty, group comparisons, categorical associations, correlation, simple linear regression, and reporting. These topics are developed in 16 teaching chapters. An introductory logistic regression chapter explains binary outcomes and odds ratios as a bridge to Volume II. Adjusted modeling, advanced diagnostic assessment, and prediction-model development belong to later volumes.
After studying this volume, the reader should be able to define the unit of observation; distinguish independent from paired observations; check data coding and missingness; choose a basic method for a specified question; interpret an estimate with its confidence interval; and write a results paragraph supported by a clear table or figure. These are the learning outcomes used throughout the manuscript.

title: Hands-On Data Analysis Using Jamovi
text:
How to use the book
Read the foundations before moving to an analysis chapter. Within each chapter, start with the question and data structure, then study the method, assumptions, illustrative example, interpretation, and reporting. Complete the review questions before checking the answers. The decision guide in the appendices supports method selection but does not replace reading the relevant chapter.
Every main chapter contains a separate Hands-on subsection and a note box. These boxes are intentionally empty in this review version. They are reserved for the author’s jamovi datasets, screenshots, saved analyses, and procedural demonstrations. The conceptual text and small numerical illustrations can be reviewed now; the complete practical workflow will be added in those boxes.
All health examples and numerical results in this manuscript are invented for teaching. They do not represent observed patient data, claims about treatment effectiveness, or clinical thresholds. A number used to illustrate a method should not be taken as a recommendation for patient care.

title: Hands-On Data Analysis Using Jamovi
text:
Reading statistical language
An outcome is the variable whose distribution or relationship is being studied. A predictor is a variable used to explain or model the outcome. These labels describe an analysis role and do not establish a causal relationship. A parameter is a population quantity; a statistic is calculated from the observed sample. An estimate is the sample-based value used to learn about a parameter.
Read a result in three parts: its direction and size, its uncertainty, and its relevance to the research question. For example, a mean difference is incomplete without the group order and measurement unit. A ratio is incomplete without its reference category. A p-value is incomplete without the model and hypothesis to which it refers. Reporting guidance is available in the SAMPL guidelines. [2]

title: Foundations
text:
The first task is to establish what the data can answer. A well-defined question identifies the population, the outcome, the comparison or predictor, and the time at which the outcome is measured. The study design then determines whether observations are independent, paired, repeated, or clustered. These decisions must precede a statistical test.
The six chapters in this part move from the research question to a usable analytical record. The first introduces designs, measurement scales, sampling, and the unit of observation. The second explains the jamovi environment. Four dedicated preparation chapters then address data entry and validation, cleaning and missing values, transformations and derived variables, and preparation for a specific analysis.
These stages have different purposes. Validation discovers discrepancies between the file and the measurement plan. Cleaning resolves them using evidence. Transformation creates quantities needed for the question. Analysis preparation defines which eligible observations and variables contribute to a particular result. Keeping those purposes explicit helps the researcher explain both the values and the denominator.
Use this part to prepare an analysis specification containing the question, eligible observations, variables, coding, missing-value rules, and intended summaries. STROBE reporting guidance asks observational researchers to describe participants, variables, bias, study size, and statistical methods explicitly. That reporting requirement is easier to meet when these items are documented before analysis. [1]
By the end of this part, the reader should be able to inspect a dataset without starting a test and identify whether its structure matches the intended analysis.




1. EQUATOR Network. STROBE: Guidelines for reporting observational studies. https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/strobe/ [accessed 5 Oct. 2026].

title: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research
text:
1.2 Start with the question
Consider three questions about an outpatient clinic: What proportion of attendees have elevated blood pressure? Does mean blood pressure differ between two treatment groups? Does blood pressure change within a patient after follow-up? These questions require different data structures and target quantities, even though all involve the same measurement.
Write the question as a sentence before naming a test. Specify who is included, what is measured, which comparison is relevant, and when the measurement occurs. For example: “Among eligible adults attending the clinic during the study period, what is the mean difference in systolic blood pressure between group A and group B at three months?” This sentence defines the population, outcome, groups, time point, and direction of the intended comparison.
The analysis objective describes what the analysis should do. Description summarises observed values. Estimation quantifies a population quantity. Comparison estimates a contrast between groups. Association examines how variables vary together. Prediction estimates an outcome for an individual or future observation. A study can contain more than one objective, but each analysis should have a defined role.
crumbs: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research

title: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research
section: 1.3 Define the population, sample, and target quantity
text:
1.3 Define the population, sample, and target quantity
The population is the set of people or observations to which the question refers. The sample is the set actually observed. A clinic sample and a community population are different targets: attendance may depend on illness, access, referral, or willingness to seek care. State the population to which the findings are intended to apply, rather than allowing the software’s sample size to define it.
A parameter describes a population quantity, such as a mean or proportion. A statistic is its sample-based counterpart. The estimand is the precise quantity the study seeks to estimate. “Difference in blood pressure” is incomplete; “mean follow-up blood pressure in A minus that in B among eligible adults” is more precise. A positive or negative value then has a defined meaning.
Record the scale of the estimand. A difference uses the original measurement unit. A proportion describes a fraction of a defined denominator. A ratio compares two quantities on a multiplicative scale. Each requires a different reporting sentence, even when the underlying research concern is similar.

This table is an orientation to data structure, not a substitute for a design-specific analysis plan. STROBE identifies the observational designs covered by its statement and the information needed to describe their conduct and analysis. [1]
Random assignment and random sampling answer different concerns. Assignment determines how study groups are formed; sampling determines how observations enter the study. A trial can randomise treatment among a selected clinic population without representing every person in the wider community. Keep the study’s internal comparison and its intended generalisation as separate judgments.
crumbs: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research

title: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research
text:
1.5 Identify the unit of observation
The unit of observation is the entity represented by one analytical record. It may be a patient, hospital admission, visit, household, or facility. It is not automatically a person. If a patient has several admissions, counting each admission creates a study of admissions unless the analysis explicitly accounts for repeated records from the same person.
For a simple independent analysis in this volume, one row usually represents one participant and each participant contributes once to the relevant comparison. For a paired analysis, the same participant contributes measurements at two times or a defined matched pair contributes two related observations. More extensive repeated or clustered structures require methods developed in later volumes.
Before analysis, complete the sentence: “One row represents …” Then count unique units as well as rows. An accidental duplicate row and a valid repeat visit can look similar in a spreadsheet, but they have different meanings and should not be handled by the same deletion rule.

In jamovi, measure type and storage type are separate properties. An integer column can contain a continuous measurement, an ordered score, a category code, or an identifier. Setting a column as nominal, ordinal, continuous, or ID determines how it is treated in analyses; a numerical code alone does not establish its measurement scale. [2]
Age recorded in years is quantitative even when stored as whole numbers. A code of 1 for a blood group is a label, not a quantity to average. A severity category coded 1, 2, and 3 is ordered, but the numerical distance between categories need not represent equal changes in severity. Preserve that distinction when choosing a method.
The role of a variable can change across questions. Age may be the outcome in a descriptive analysis and a predictor in a regression. Its measurement type remains the same; its analytical role changes. Define both properties in the data dictionary.

1.6.1 Interval and ratio measurement scales
An interval scale has meaningful equal differences but an arbitrary zero. Celsius temperature is a familiar example: a ten-degree difference has meaning, but 20°C is not twice the temperature of 10°C. A ratio scale also has a meaningful zero, allowing ratios such as one measured length being twice another. The distinction concerns the measurement definition, not how many decimal places are stored. [3]
Nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio are the classical scale categories. Quantitative data can also be discrete, such as a count, or treated as continuous, such as a length measurement. These classifications answer different questions: ordering and meaningful arithmetic on one hand, and the set of possible numerical values on the other.

title: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research
text:
1.7 Sampling, uncertainty, and bias
Sampling variability means that repeated samples could give different estimates. A standard error or confidence interval addresses this variation under stated assumptions. A systematic measurement error, selective inclusion, or unaddressed confounding is a different problem. A narrow interval around a biased estimate remains misleading.
Use a simple thought experiment. Suppose a weighing scale adds two kilograms to every reading. Collecting many measurements can make the sample mean very precise, while the systematic two-kilogram error remains. The remedy is to check the measurement process; merely increasing the sample size does not correct the instrument.
Similarly, a large clinic dataset may describe clinic attendees well while failing to represent people who never attend. In the report, distinguish the uncertainty quantified by the statistical method from limitations in how the observations were obtained. Confidence intervals are conditional on the analysis assumptions and do not automatically include every source of uncertainty. [4]
crumbs: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research

title: 1  Role of Statistics in Health Research
text:
1.8 Establish an analysis workflow
Start by specifying the question and design. Create a data dictionary and preserve the source file. Check records, coding, units, missingness, and eligibility. Describe the observed data and inspect relevant graphs. Select the estimand and method, examine assumptions, then interpret the estimate and its uncertainty. Finally, write the result and retain the analysis file and decision log.
The workflow should leave an audit trail. Record a change because it is justified by a coding definition or verified source, not because it improves a p-value. Record an exclusion because it follows the study rules, not because an observation is inconvenient. A documented decision can later be examined and revised; an undocumented change is difficult to reconstruct.

Define the analytical unit and whether repeated visits from the same patient are relevant and dependent. A study of patients and a study of visits have different denominators.
Establish what the categories mean and whether the scale has a justified quantitative interpretation. Numerical codes do not establish equal spacing.
Selection, measurement, and other systematic problems may remain. Greater precision does not establish representativeness or correct a biased measurement process.

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
text:
2.2 The purpose of the software
jamovi provides a spreadsheet-style data view and an analysis interface with results displayed alongside the data. Its official introductory guidance describes importing data, setting variable properties, running an analysis, and saving the data and analysis together in an .omv file. [1]
Treat the software as an environment for implementing an analysis plan. It can calculate results once variables and options are assigned, but it cannot determine whether the study question, population, eligibility rules, or causal interpretation are appropriate. A result appearing in the output panel confirms that a calculation was performed; it does not by itself validate the analysis.

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
text:
2.3 Installation and version information
Obtain jamovi from the official website, https://www.jamovi.org. The author’s Hands-on demonstration should identify the operating system, jamovi version, and any additional module used. The same analysis name can be available through different modules, and software updates can alter defaults or output labels.
Record versions at the beginning of a project and when an analysis is repeated after an update. If two researchers obtain different results, compare the data, variable settings, selected options, missing-data handling, and versions before assuming that one numerical result is wrong. Reproducibility requires matching these choices.
The learning aim is to understand the meaning of an option before selecting it. For example, selecting a confidence interval does not change the research question; it requests an uncertainty summary. Changing the reference category changes the direction of a reported contrast. These options have different analytical consequences.

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
text:
2.4 Understand the interface
The data area contains observations and variables. The variable editor defines properties such as the name, data type, measure type, and levels. The analysis area assigns variables and options to a method. The results area displays tables and other output. The spreadsheet documentation explains the distinction between data variables, computed variables, and transformed variables. [2]
Use the data view to verify what will enter an analysis. Use the analysis options to verify what calculation is requested. Use the output to inspect the resulting estimate, sample size, uncertainty, and assumptions. Each area answers a different question, so a complete review should examine all three.
An automatically updated result can be useful during exploration, but it also means that a later change to the data or a filter can change previously generated output. Save dated versions at important review points and record intentional changes. Do not treat a screenshot as a substitute for the file that generated it.

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
text:
2.5 Importing and structuring data
Prepare the source file with one header row, one variable per column, and one record per defined observation unit. Avoid merged cells, embedded totals, decorative headings, and values that combine a number with a unit in the same cell. A column of values such as “120 mmHg” requires a clear conversion to numeric values before being treated as a continuous measurement.
Maintain a source copy before changing the imported data. Compare the imported number of rows and variables with the expected source dimensions. Inspect several records at the beginning and end of the file, as well as unusual values, rather than assuming that a successful import preserved the intended meaning of every column.
Use short, stable variable names with descriptions for their full meaning. For example, sbp_followup can have the description “Systolic blood pressure at the three-month visit, mmHg.” A clear name helps identify the variable in analysis dialogs, while the description preserves its definition.

What to verify

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
text:
2.6 Variable properties and levels
Check the measure type after importing. Imported values can be stored as integer, decimal, or text, while their measure type may be nominal, ordinal, continuous, or ID. jamovi may infer properties on opening a file, so the researcher should verify them against the dictionary. [3]
An outcome such as blood pressure should retain its measurement unit and continuous meaning. A grouping variable should display its category labels. A participant identifier should link records rather than act as a predictor solely because it contains numbers. For an ordinal variable, inspect the order of the levels as well as their labels.
Reference categories require particular care. If an analysis reports group B relative to A, the sign or ratio direction differs from A relative to B. Write the intended comparison before reading the output. Later chapters show how this direction affects mean differences, correlation, and odds ratios.

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
text:
2.7 Saving data and analyses
A plain data file and a saved analysis file serve different purposes. A CSV can provide an accessible rectangular data source, but it does not preserve the complete set of jamovi analyses and options. The .omv format saves the jamovi project information needed to reopen the analysis. [1]
Keep three related items: the unchanged source file, a documented analysis-ready file, and the saved jamovi analysis. Give each an understandable name and version date. For example, an author may distinguish clinic_source, clinic_clean_v01, and clinic_analysis_v01; the exact naming convention is less important than its consistent use.
When sharing a result for review, include the analysis file, data dictionary, and a short record of exclusions and transformations. A screenshot can help explain a table, but another researcher should be able to examine the underlying variables and options as well.

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
text:
2.8 Reviewing an output before interpretation
Read the analysis title and verify that it matches the intended method. Check the variables and sample size. Identify the estimate and its direction. Locate the confidence interval, test statistic, degrees of freedom where applicable, and p-value. Check any note about missing values, assumptions, or estimation failure.
Suppose a table contains 80 observations although the imported file has 100 records. Possible explanations include missing values, an active filter, or an analysis limited to one subgroup. Determine which explanation applies before interpreting the estimate. The difference between imported records and analysed observations must be understandable.
Do not copy every software table into a manuscript. Retain the output for verification, then choose the quantities needed to answer the research question. A reader-facing table has a defined purpose and usually requires clearer labels than those used in the analysis window.

title: 2  Getting Started with jamovi
section: 2.9 R as a later reproducibility layer
text:
2.9 R as a later reproducibility layer
jamovi offers syntax mode and Rj for working with R. These provide routes to code-based analysis, with package and environment requirements that should be checked when they are used. The availability of R integration does not mean that every method proposed for the series is supplied by the default interface. [4]
For Volume I, begin with transparent data definitions, saved analyses, and recorded options. The project’s verification script separately reproduces the small numerical illustrations using base R; it is not a replacement for the author’s future jamovi demonstrations. Later volumes develop a fuller relationship between graphical analysis and code.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
text: After this chapter, the reader should be able to define what one row represents, build a usable data dictionary, distinguish data type from measure type, specify entry checks, and verify that an imported file retains its intended values and structure.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
text:
3.2 Start with the measurement plan
Data entry is the conversion of recorded observations into a structured analytical file. Validation asks whether that conversion follows the study’s definitions. A file can open successfully and still contain the wrong unit, a truncated identifier, or a category whose code has changed meaning. Successful import is therefore the beginning of validation.
Before entering data, identify the source, population, observation unit, measurement occasion, and expected number of records. Specify who records each item and how unclear source entries will be resolved. The questionnaire, case record form, and data dictionary should use compatible definitions. An analysis cannot distinguish a missing measurement from an unrecorded negative result if the collection form did not preserve that distinction.
The four preparation chapters have separate responsibilities. This chapter covers capture and validation. Chapter 4 addresses verified corrections and missingness. Chapter 5 develops derived variables. Chapter 6 assembles the variables, eligible observations, and settings needed for a particular analysis.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
section: 3.3 Define the row and its identifier
text:
3.3 Define the row and its identifier
A row may represent a participant, visit, admission, specimen, household, or event. State its meaning before choosing an identifier. A participant-level file ordinarily needs a unique participant ID. A visit-level file may need the combination of participant ID and visit occasion to identify a row uniquely.
An identifier links records; its numerical appearance does not make it a quantitative measurement. The ID 0017 may be different from 17 in a source system. Preserve the intended format during entry and import. Do not use the current row number as a substitute for a stable identifier, because sorting or inserting records can change that number.
For paired measurements, the same row must contain measurements from the same participant, or a verified key must link the separate files. A convenient row order does not establish matching. For clustered data, retain the cluster identifier even when the current volume’s simple methods cannot accommodate the full dependence structure.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
text:
3.4 Build the data dictionary
The dictionary should allow another researcher to interpret a column without asking the person who entered it. Include the name, definition, source, timing, unit, data and measure types, permitted values, missing codes, and any validation rule. A derived variable also needs its formula and the version of its source variables.

The blood pressure entries intentionally contain no invented clinical acceptance limit. A project’s limits should come from its measurement protocol and instrument, and should distinguish an error from a value that needs review.
Use short, stable variable names and informative descriptions. Keep units out of the cells containing numeric values: store 128, with mmHg in the dictionary, rather than mixing 128 mmHg and 128 in one column. Store a categorical response in its own column instead of using cell colour to encode its meaning. These principles are consistent with recommendations for organising spreadsheet data. [1]

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
section: 3.5 Separate data type from measure type
text:
3.5 Separate data type from measure type
The data type describes how values are stored. jamovi distinguishes integer, decimal, and text data. The measure type describes how a variable should be treated: continuous, ordinal, nominal, or ID. The automatic choices made during import need review against the dictionary. [2]
A study group coded 1 and 2 is nominal, because subtracting the codes has no scientific meaning. A count stored as an integer may be used as a quantitative variable, but that storage choice does not make every statistical model appropriate. An ordinal severity score retains order without establishing equal distances between categories.
Check category labels as well as codes. If 1 means present in one source and absent in another, the same stored value has different meanings. Establish a common mapping from the dictionaries before combining files. Record the reference group and ordinal order explicitly; they affect the presentation and interpretation of later results.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
text:
3.6 Choose a consistent table structure
Keep one header row, one variable per column, and one value per cell in a rectangular entry table. Put explanatory notes, totals, and presentation tables elsewhere. Avoid merged cells, repeated headers within the data, and blank rows used to separate groups. They describe a visual layout rather than an analytical structure. [1]
Wide format places different measurement occasions in separate columns for the same participant. This is a useful starting structure for the simple paired procedures in Volume I. Long format places occasions in separate rows and preserves an ID and time variable. Neither arrangement removes dependence between measurements from one participant.

Keep the source structure when it contains information that a later analysis needs. Reducing repeated visits to one outcome is an analytical decision with a selection rule, rather than a routine formatting operation.

section: 3.7 Use checks at entry and after entry
text:
3.7 Use checks at entry and after entry
Validation rules should be specified before viewing the statistical results. Their role is to detect departures from the collection definitions, rather than force the dataset to fit a preferred distribution.








Check
Example of what it detects
Required response

Data format

A hard rule concerns a contradiction with the definition, such as a negative count of events. A review rule flags a value whose validity requires evidence, such as an unusually high measurement. A flag is not itself an instruction to delete the observation. Keep the rule, source query, and eventual decision traceable.
Some entry systems allow limits and permitted categories to be enforced immediately. A spreadsheet or imported file still needs a separate validation pass. Independent double entry or a targeted source check may be appropriate when the error consequences justify the effort. Record the verification coverage; checking a sample does not establish that every value was checked.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
section: 3.8 Distinguish missing, zero, and not applicable
text:
3.8 Distinguish missing, zero, and not applicable
Zero is a value. Missing means that the intended value is unavailable. Not applicable means that the item does not apply under a defined rule. An event count of zero among observed participants is different from an unknown event count, and both differ from a measurement that was never required.
Keep a numeric measurement column suitable for calculation and record missing reasons in a separate field when those reasons matter. A reason might distinguish an absent visit, a failed measurement, and a participant outside the eligible measurement group. Do not use a numeric zero for all three situations.
jamovi represents missing values as blank cells. If a source uses a special code, define that code as missing in the variable settings or create a documented cleaned variable before analysis. Otherwise the code may be treated as an ordinary value. [2] A special code is missing because the dictionary says so, rather than because it is inconvenient for the analysis.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
text:
3.9 Verify the import
Preserve the source file and import a named working copy. Note the source version, export format, delimiter, decimal convention, and date convention. Inspect whether quoted text, accented labels, leading zeros, and blank cells have survived the transfer. If a date such as 05/06/2026 is ambiguous, resolve its convention from the source rather than from whichever interpretation produces a plausible chronology.
Compare expected and imported records, variables, and category counts. Inspect a few source values from the beginning, middle, and end of the file, including values that challenge the format: a decimal, a special missing code, an identifier with leading zeros, and a label containing punctuation. Reconcile discrepancies before calculating results.
An imported numeric column may be text if some cells include units or unexpected characters. Converting the whole column without investigating those cells can create new missing values. Document the number of conversions that succeed and fail, and verify that no genuine observations disappeared unnoticed.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
text:
3.10 An invented validation audit

Suppose an entry file is expected to contain 120 participants and 12 specified variables. It imports with 120 rows and 12 columns. A further audit identifies two rows sharing an ID, four uses of the undeclared group label b, and three follow-up fields containing the dictionary’s missing code 999.

The matching row and column counts do not establish validity. Query the repeated ID before deciding whether it represents a duplicate or an incorrect identifier. Confirm whether b means group B before harmonising it. Define 999 as missing according to the dictionary and retain the reason if available. The issues may overlap within participants, so adding 2, 4, and 3 does not necessarily count the number of affected people.
Write the audit finding before correcting the working file. The next chapter explains how to resolve and log the findings. Validation discovers an issue; cleaning implements a supported decision.

title: 3  Data Entry and Validation
text:
3.11 Release a validated entry file
Before handover, confirm the observation unit and keys, reconcile record counts, verify variable properties, inspect categories and missing codes, and list unresolved queries. Save the dictionary with the entry file. A reviewer should know whether the file is ready for cleaning or whether source questions remain.
For reporting, describe the collection and validation process at the level needed to assess the data. A statement such as “Data were checked” is insufficient when the relevant questions concern matching, eligibility, or conflicting measurements. The later reporting chapter explains how these preparation decisions enter the methods section.

A row may be duplicated, may represent a repeat visit, or may contain an incorrect ID. Count participants using a verified key and the defined observation unit.
The scientific meaning determines the measure type. Group membership is nominal even when its stored codes are numbers.
An unusual observation can be valid. Resolve it against the source and protocol, and retain a record of the decision.

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
section: 4.2 Cleaning is a documented decision process
text:
4.2 Cleaning is a documented decision process
Cleaning changes an analytical representation when an issue has been identified and a supported resolution is available. It includes correcting a transcription error, harmonising equivalent labels, recognising special missing codes, and resolving duplicated records. Each action needs a reason that another researcher can inspect.
Keep the original export unchanged and work on a named copy. Record the source version and the dictionary used to interpret it. Save the rules and change log with the cleaned file. Preserving a raw file separately from analytical work is part of good spreadsheet organisation. [1]
The aim is to represent the recorded observations correctly. A cleaner distribution, a larger analytical sample, or a smaller p-value is not evidence that a correction is valid. When a finding cannot be resolved, retain its status and explain how it will affect the analysis.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
section: 4.3 Classify the finding before changing the value
text:
4.3 Classify the finding before changing the value
Separate confirmed errors, equivalent representations, valid unusual observations, and unresolved queries. They require different responses.








Finding
Evidence needed
Suitable action




Transcription error
Source confirms a different value
Correct the working value and log the change


Equivalent category labels
Dictionary confirms a common meaning
Apply a consistent label mapping


Special missing code
Dictionary defines the code
Represent it as missing for calculation


Valid unusual observation
Source and measurement definition support it
Retain it; assess influence if relevant


Unresolved conflicting values
Available sources do not settle the discrepancy

Do not guess that a large value is a misplaced decimal point. Query the source. If it confirms the recorded value, the statistical analysis must accommodate or transparently assess it. If it confirms an error, correct that error because of the source evidence, even if the result is almost unchanged.

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
section: 4.4 Resolve duplicates using the correct key
text:
4.4 Resolve duplicates using the correct key
In a participant-level file, an ID repeated twice is a query. In a visit-level file, the same ID can appear legitimately at several occasions. The combination of ID and visit may be the correct row key. Check the observation unit defined in Chapter 3 before removing anything.
An exact duplicate has the same relevant values and key as another record. A conflicting duplicate shares a key but contains different values. The latter requires source review; retaining the first or last row by default can select an arbitrary measurement.
Suppose an invented file contains 204 rows expected to represent one row per participant. Source review establishes that four rows are repeated exports of existing records, leaving 200 distinct participant records. This arithmetic is valid only after confirming what those four rows represent. A file with 204 legitimate visits from 200 participants would require a different interpretation.
If several measurements are eligible, use a defined selection rule, such as a protocol’s scheduled occasion and allowed time window. Record tie handling. Averaging repeated measurements or choosing one is a derivation with consequences for the target quantity; it is not merely duplicate removal.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
section: 4.5 Harmonise categories without changing their meaning
text:
4.5 Harmonise categories without changing their meaning
Inspect frequency tables before and after recoding. Differences in case, spacing, or spelling may produce separate labels for the same category. Confirm equivalence from the dictionary or source, then map them to a defined common label.
For example, B, b, and Group B may represent the same study group. Unknown and No do not represent the same event status. A text value such as NA is also ambiguous until the source explains whether it means missing, not applicable, or a legitimate category.
Preserve the original label when the mapping needs an audit. Compare original and cleaned variables in a cross-tabulation. Verify that every intended category has a destination, and inspect values left unmapped. A new label alone cannot demonstrate that the recode worked.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
section: 4.6 Check units, dates, and internal consistency
text:
4.6 Check units, dates, and internal consistency
A measurement can be numerically plausible while using the wrong unit. Review the source unit and dictionary before conversion. When a column combines values measured in centimetres and metres, an additional unit field or reliable source record is needed to determine which conversion applies. Guessing from the magnitude can misclassify valid observations.
Check chronology against the study definitions. A recorded follow-up before baseline can indicate an entry error, an incorrect visit label, or a source-system convention. Confirm the explanation before calculating elapsed time. Preserve the original date representation and specify the parsing rule used in any external preparation step.
Cross-field checks should reflect the collection process. An event date outside the defined observation period is a query about the outcome definition. A total that differs from the sum of recorded components is a query about calculation or measurement. Record the resolved values and the evidence, rather than silently forcing consistency.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
text:
4.7 Distinguish missingness from exclusion
An ineligible participant is outside a stated analysis population. A participant with a missing outcome may be eligible but lack the value needed for a particular calculation. A verified duplicate is an extra representation of an existing observation. These are different reasons for changing a record count.
Retain reason fields so the counts can be reported separately. If several exclusion criteria overlap, use a stated order for a sequential flow and also retain the underlying flags. Summing overlapping flags does not necessarily equal the number excluded.
Missingness should be described among the observations for which the measurement was intended. Report the eligible number, observed number, and missing number. If not-applicable observations are excluded from that denominator, explain the rule.

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
text:
4.8 An invented sample-flow example
The following counts illustrate documentation; they do not describe an included patient dataset. Begin with the 200 distinct participant records from the duplicate example. Eight fail the specified eligibility criteria, leaving 192 eligible participants. Among these, 12 lack the follow-up outcome, leaving 180 available values for that outcome.








Stage
Number
Meaning




Imported rows
204
Includes four verified duplicate rows


Distinct participants
200
Duplicate resolution completed


Eligible participants
192
Eight distinct participants are ineligible


Observed follow-up outcomes
180
Twelve eligible participants lack this outcome



The missing-outcome percentage among eligible participants is 12/192\times100=6.25\%. The 180 observed outcomes represent 93.75% of eligible participants. The missing proportion is not 12/204, because imported rows are not the relevant eligible participant denominator.
Suppose the eligible groups each contain 96 participants. Four outcomes are missing in A and eight in B, leaving 92 and 88 observed values. The group-specific missing proportions are 4.17% and 8.33%. A similar overall percentage could hide a different pattern between groups.
These counts can describe the missingness pattern. They cannot establish that the missing outcomes would have the same distribution as observed outcomes. Interpretation requires information about follow-up and reasons for absence.

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
text:
4.9 Understand assumptions about missingness
Missing completely at random (MCAR) means that the missingness process is unrelated to observed and unobserved values. Missing at random (MAR) means that, conditional on relevant observed information, missingness does not depend on the missing values. Missing not at random (MNAR) means that dependence on unobserved values remains. These are properties and assumptions of the data process, rather than conclusions obtained from the percentage of blank cells. [2]
A missed visit caused by an administrative accident may have a different relationship with health status from a missed visit caused by worsening illness. Even when a reason is recorded, its implications require judgment. Observed associations with missingness can challenge a simple assumption, but absence of such associations does not establish that unseen values are irrelevant.
Record known reasons, examine missingness by group or occasion, and identify which assumptions the intended analysis needs. Formal missing-data modeling and sensitivity analysis belong beyond the introductory workflow in this volume.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
text:
4.10 Know what complete-case analysis does
A complete-case analysis includes observations that have the values needed for its specified variables. A follow-up group comparison may use 180 outcomes in the invented example, while a paired analysis may use fewer if some baseline values are also missing. Missingness in an unrelated variable need not exclude a participant from the first calculation.
R’s complete.cases identifies observations without missing values in the supplied variables. The variables supplied therefore determine the case definition. [3] jamovi analyses also offer different missing-data handling choices in some procedures; inspect the relevant analysis settings and the resulting sample size. [4]
Complete-case analysis changes the analysed set and may change the population represented by the result. Its validity depends on the missingness process, design, and target quantity. A large retained sample is not sufficient proof that bias is negligible.
State which variables defined completeness, how many observations were omitted, and what is known about their missingness. If the same analysis is compared across different models, explain whether the sample changed as well as the model.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
section: 4.11 Why simple replacement is not a neutral repair
text:
4.11 Why simple replacement is not a neutral repair
Replacing an unknown value with zero turns absence of information into an observed measurement. Replacing every missing outcome with the sample mean creates repeated invented values and suppresses the variation that those outcomes might have contained. Neither action restores the lost information.
Carrying a previous measurement forward also imposes a substantive assumption about change. It should not be described as an ordinary cleaning step. An imputation procedure needs a rationale, an appropriate uncertainty calculation, and assumptions that match the study. [2]
For this introductory workflow, resolve coding errors, preserve actual missingness, report the analytical sample, and acknowledge the limitation. Seek an appropriate missing-data strategy when the intended research conclusion depends materially on unavailable values.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

title: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values
text:
4.12 Handle unusual observations transparently
Use summaries and graphs to locate values for review, but use evidence to decide whether they are errors. A boxplot flag or a large standardised distance is a description of an observation relative to the sample, not proof that the observation is invalid.
A confirmed unusual value can have substantial influence on a mean or fitted line. An additional analysis examining that influence may be informative when justified and labelled. Report the main analysis rule and the sensitivity result; do not replace the primary result silently because an alternative is more convenient.
Deleting valid extreme values changes the analysed distribution and can change the target population. An exclusion rule should follow the design or a defensible measurement rule and should be stated before selecting results.
crumbs: 4  Data Cleaning and Missing Values

section: 4.13 Keep a change log and a release record
text:
4.13 Keep a change log and a release record
A useful log includes the file version, affected key or variable, issue, supporting source, action, reason, date, and reviewer. Keep identifying details limited to what the authorised review process requires.



Log field
Example entry for a teaching file




Issue

Verification

Action
Map b to B in the cleaned group column


Check
Original-by-cleaned table has no unintended mapping


Record

Before release, reconcile row and participant counts, repeat range and category checks, compare missingness with the raw file, and list unresolved issues. A corrected missing code may increase the recognised missing count even though no information was lost during cleaning. Explain that change.
The cleaned file is ready for derivation when its values and structure have been reviewed. It is ready for a particular analysis only after the population, required variables, matching, and exclusion settings have also been checked in Chapter 6.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
section: 5.2 Define the purpose before the formula
text:
5.2 Define the purpose before the formula
A derived variable expresses a quantity needed for the research question. A change score, a unit conversion, an ordered category, and a logarithm are different operations with different meanings. Write the intended definition in words before implementing its formula.
Keep the source columns. Give the derived column a distinct name and a description containing its unit, direction, formula, permissible inputs, and missing-value rule. Record why the derivation is needed and whether it was specified before examining the outcomes.
Cleaning resolves a supported representation problem. Transformation creates a new representation for an analytical purpose. Correcting a verified transcription error is cleaning; calculating follow-up minus baseline is derivation. A mathematical transformation does not repair invalid source values or make an unsuitable study design valid.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
section: 5.3 Computed and transformed variables in jamovi
text:
5.3 Computed and transformed variables in jamovi
jamovi’s computed variables create columns from formulas involving existing variables. Transformed variables allow a reusable rule to be applied to source columns. A transformation refers to its selected source with $source, and recode conditions are evaluated in order, using the first condition that is true. [1, 2]
The chapter uses small formula illustrations. They are not results from an included dataset or a tested saved jamovi analysis. The author will add version-specific demonstrations and screenshots in the reserved Hands-on section.
Choose the tool according to the derivation. A difference between two specified columns is naturally a computed variable. Reversing several items on the same response scale can use one reusable transformation. In either case, the formula needs independent checks before it supports a reported result.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
section: 5.4 Distinguish calculations within a row from column summaries
text:
5.4 Distinguish calculations within a row from column summaries
A row calculation uses values belonging to one observation. A column summary uses a set of observations. Confusing these levels can produce a syntactically valid but scientifically wrong variable.
For example, the mean of three specified questionnaire items within a participant differs from the mean response to one item across participants. Likewise, an individual’s change from baseline differs from the difference between two column means when the columns contain different observed participants.
The documented jamovi function names distinguish several row and variable operations: MEAN(...) and SUM(...) are row functions, whereas VMEAN(var) and VSUM(var) summarise a column. Z(var) standardises a variable, and LN(var) takes natural logarithms. [3] Check the function’s input and missing-value behaviour against the intended rule; a function name alone does not define a valid score.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
text:
5.5 Unit conversion and ratios
Convert only when the original unit is known. A height of 160 cm becomes 1.60 m by dividing by 100. Retain the source height and label the converted column in metres. Do not combine units in one column and infer the unit solely from magnitude.
Body mass index uses weight in kilograms divided by squared height in metres. [4] An invented illustration uses a weight of 80 kg and a height of 1.60 m:

\mathrm{BMI}=\frac{\mathrm{weight\ in\ kg}}{(\mathrm{height\ in\ m})^2}
=\frac{80}{1.60^2}=31.25\ \mathrm{kg/m^2}.

This is a derivation example, without a clinical classification. Inserting 160 instead of 1.60 gives 0.003125, showing why unit verification must precede calculation. A zero, missing, or unresolved height cannot produce a valid BMI; investigate the source rather than treating an infinite or absent result as a new measured value.
A ratio also requires a meaningful denominator. A rate per unit time requires observed time in the stated unit. When the denominator is zero or unknown, define how the result is represented and what the source problem means. Do not silently convert an undefined ratio to zero.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
text:
5.6 Change scores and direction
For paired baseline and follow-up measurements, define

d=\mathrm{follow\!\text{-}\!up}-\mathrm{baseline}.

With this definition, negative values indicate a lower follow-up measurement. The formula illustration sbp_followup - sbp_baseline uses columns belonging to the same participant. Verify matching before calculating it.
For invented baseline and follow-up values of 146 and 138 mmHg, the change is -8 mmHg. Reversing the subtraction gives +8 mmHg. The statistical evidence can be equivalent under a consistent sign change, but the reporting language must follow the stated direction.
An individual’s percentage change, when baseline is a valid non-zero denominator, is

100\times\frac{\mathrm{follow\!\text{-}\!up}-\mathrm{baseline}}{\mathrm{baseline}}.

For those values it is -5.48%. Percentage change and absolute change answer different questions. A smaller baseline can produce a larger percentage change for the same absolute difference. When baseline is zero, the ratio is undefined. When baseline is missing, no observed within-person percentage change exists.
The average of individual percentage changes is also generally different from the percentage change in the two group means. Define which quantity is being reported. Preserve enough information to reproduce that calculation.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
text:
5.7 Recode categories with explicit boundaries
Recoding needs a complete mapping, not just a new name. Specify the destination for each permitted source category and the treatment of missing or unexpected values. Verify the mapping with an original-by-derived table.
For an invented waiting-time categorisation, define three groups without implying a clinical threshold:








Source value, minutes
Derived category
Boundary check




0\leq x<10
Shorter
0 belongs here; 10 does not


10\leq x<20
Intermediate
10 belongs here; 20 does not


x\geq20
Longer
20 belongs here


Missing or invalid input
Missing or flagged for review
Do not label it as a valid shorter wait



Check values just below, exactly at, and just above each boundary. Mutually exclusive conditions avoid ambiguity. If a procedure uses the first true rule, a broad condition placed first can make later conditions unreachable. [2]
Categorisation removes distinctions within each category. Values of 10 and 19.9 become identical under the invented middle category, while 19.9 and 20 become different despite their small separation. Dichotomising a continuous variable can discard information and reduce statistical power. [5]
Use a category when its definition serves the question, with a stated source or purpose. Retain the original continuous variable. Do not search repeatedly for the threshold that produces the preferred result.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
text:
5.8 Reverse scoring and composite scores
For an item coded from a minimum a to a maximum b, reversal is

x_{\mathrm{reversed}}=a+b-x.

On an invented 1-to-5 response scale, this becomes 6-x: 1 maps to 5, 2 to 4, and 3 remains 3. A reusable jamovi transformation can express this as 6 - $source. [2] Recognise declared missing codes before reversal; a missing code of 99 should not become a score of -93.
Reversal is justified by the scoring specification, not by whether it improves an internal consistency statistic. For an established instrument, follow its permitted item coding, scoring, and missing-item rules. Correct arithmetic does not establish that an invented item set measures a valid construct.
Suppose three invented items, after correct reversal where required, have scores 4, 5, and 3. Their sum is 12 and their mean is 4. If one item is missing, a sum of only the two available items is not comparable with a complete three-item sum. An available-item mean also makes assumptions about what the missing item represents.
State the minimum number of required items and the procedure when that minimum is not met. A prorated or available-item score is a deliberate rule that needs justification; it should not arise accidentally from a function’s default handling of blanks. Verify complete, partly missing, and entirely missing examples separately.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
section: 5.9 Logarithms change the scale of the question
text:
5.9 Logarithms change the scale of the question
The natural logarithm is defined for positive values. For a positive variable x, the transformed value is \ln(x); the original scale is recovered with \exp(\ln(x))=x. The documented jamovi function LN(var) performs the natural-log calculation. [3]
On the log scale, equal ratios give equal differences. Increasing from 10 to 20 and from 20 to 40 gives the same log difference, \ln(2)=0.6931, despite different absolute increases. This can be useful when multiplicative relationships match the scientific question.
Transforming individual values also changes the meaning of an average. For the invented positive values 10 and 40, the arithmetic mean is 25. The mean of their natural logs, back-transformed, is 20, the geometric mean. It is not a new way to calculate the arithmetic mean.
Zero and negative values need substantive attention before a log transformation. Adding a constant merely to make the calculation possible changes the resulting scale and interpretation. Adding 1 in one measurement unit need not have the same effect after converting to another unit. Explain the chosen definition rather than treating it as a universal repair.
A transformation may improve the suitability of a model for its intended relationship, but it should not be selected only to pass a normality test. Inspect the transformed distribution and, when modeling, the relevant residual behaviour. Later chapters connect those checks with the method’s assumptions.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
text:
5.10 Standardisation and its reference set
A sample z-score is

z_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{s},

where the mean and SD refer to a stated set of observations. For an invented value of 140 mmHg, reference mean 130, and reference SD 10, the z-score is 1. The score describes relative position in that reference distribution; it does not define a clinical diagnosis.
Record whether the reference comes from all eligible observations, a group, or an external population. If the reference mean or SD changes, the same measurement receives a different score. A column with zero SD cannot be standardised by this formula.
Active filters can matter for calculations involving column summaries. jamovi’s filter documentation describes how sequential filters affect the observations used in subsequent calculations. [6] Verify the actual reference set when saving standardised variables. A value derived under one filter state should not be described as based on a different sample.

title: 5  Transformations and Derived Variables
text:
5.11 Verify and document the derivation
Check simple values by hand, both boundaries of recodes, missing inputs, invalid inputs, and the range and distribution of the new variable. Compare selected derived values with an independent calculation. Reconcile the number of missing results with the rule rather than assuming every new blank is expected.
For a change score, confirm direction and matching. For a unit conversion, confirm the factor and output unit. For a category, inspect the mapping. For a score, check item reversal and missing-item eligibility. For a log, count non-positive inputs before interpreting the transformed values.
Keep full useful precision in the analytical column and round for presentation. Rounding before deriving a boundary category or a difference can change the classification or result. Record the transformation definition with the dictionary so a reviewer can rebuild it from the source variables.

section: 6.2 A cleaned file does not define every analysis
text:
6.2 A cleaned file does not define every analysis
A reviewed dataset can support several questions, each using different variables and observations. Describing a follow-up measurement, comparing paired measurements, and fitting a relationship with age do not necessarily use the same sample. Analysis preparation makes those differences explicit before interpreting results.
The process starts with the research question and target quantity. State who is eligible, what one observation represents, which outcome is being analysed, which comparison or predictor is relevant, and at what time the outcome is measured. Then select a method that matches that specification.
Do not begin by trying every procedure that accepts the columns. The software’s acceptance of a variable does not establish that the variable has the right role, that observations are independent, or that the result answers the intended question.

title: 6  Preparing Data for a Specific Analysis
text:
6.3 Write a short analysis specification
The specification connects the design to the analytical file. It can be brief, but it must contain enough information to reproduce the included observations, variable definitions, method, and contrast direction.
The following specification is invented for an unadjusted follow-up comparison:







Component
Stated decision




Question
How does mean follow-up systolic blood pressure differ between eligible groups A and B?


Outcome
The protocol-defined follow-up measurement, in mmHg


Observation unit
One eligible participant, contributing once


Comparison
A minus B


Analytical sample
Eligible participants with known group and observed follow-up outcome


Method
Welch independent-samples comparison, if the design and data support its use


Descriptive output
Group-specific n, mean, SD, missing count, and distribution plots


Main result
Mean difference with 95% CI, followed by the test result


Limitation
An unadjusted comparison does not account for baseline or other group differences



This specification does not assert that the assumptions have already passed. It identifies what must be checked and what the result will mean. Where the study requires a baseline-adjusted or other multivariable analysis, the simple comparison is insufficient as the final model; those methods are developed in Volume II.
Distinguish a prespecified primary analysis from an exploratory analysis. If the plan changes because of a data issue, record what changed and why. Do not describe a choice made after inspecting several results as if it had been fixed beforehand.

title: 6  Preparing Data for a Specific Analysis
text:
6.5 Preserve the unit of observation
A file with one row per visit can contain more rows than participants. An independent t-test applied to all those rows would ordinarily fail to account for the relationship between visits from the same person. A matching ID does not make the ordinary independent procedure handle that dependence automatically.
Specify whether the question concerns participants, visits, or another unit. If one measurement per participant is required, select it using a justified occasion rule and document how conflicts are resolved. If repeated observations are part of the question, use a method that models their structure rather than deleting the dependence from the description.
Similarly, participants sampled within households or clinics may share cluster-level influences. Preserve the cluster variables and identify when the simple independent methods in this volume are insufficient. A larger row count cannot compensate for an inappropriate independence assumption.

title: 6  Preparing Data for a Specific Analysis
text:
6.6 Define eligibility before activating filters
An eligibility rule determines which observations belong to the target analysis population. Write it in words and implement it using defined variables. Separate eligibility from the availability of measurements needed for a particular calculation.
For example, first identify eligible participants, then determine which have the follow-up outcome. Record both counts. If an unknown eligibility field is encountered, resolve it or state the handling rule; treating an unknown value as an automatic yes or no can change the target population.
jamovi row filters exclude observations from analyses without requiring deletion of the source records. The filter state can therefore change existing results. Multiple filters and calculations involving column summaries need attention to their order and reference set. [1]
Check every active filter when the displayed sample size is unexpected. Record its expression, purpose, and included and excluded counts. An eligibility filter for one question may be inappropriate for another question in the same file. Save separate analysis files or clearly documented filter states when necessary to avoid confusing their samples.
Do not hide an analytical exclusion inside an unexplained derived column. If a value has been made missing to implement a subset, that is part of the inclusion rule and must be recorded as such.

title: 6  Preparing Data for a Specific Analysis
section: 6.7 Account for missing values for the selected variables
text:
6.7 Account for missing values for the selected variables
The required-variable list defines what completeness means. A descriptive summary of age does not necessarily require an observed follow-up outcome. A paired blood pressure comparison requires both defined measurements. A correlation requires an observed value of each variable for the same participant.
Inspect the sample count reported by each analysis and reconcile it with the eligibility and missing-value rules. jamovi’s one-way documentation, for example, distinguishes per-analysis and listwise exclusion options. [2] Different procedures and options should not be assumed to use identical cases.
When comparing models or tables, state whether differences arise from the method, the selected variables, or the analysed participants. Holding the sample constant can sometimes help isolate a model comparison, but it also excludes observations and needs a stated purpose. It is not an automatic requirement for every descriptive result.

6.8 An invented complete-pair audit
Consider a separate teaching example with 120 eligible participants. Six have no baseline measurement, eight have no follow-up measurement, and two lack both. There are 114 available baseline values and 112 available follow-up values, but neither number gives the complete-pair count.
The number lacking at least one measurement is 6+8-2=12, because the two who lack both were counted twice in the sum. The paired analysis therefore has 120-12=108 complete pairs.

For these 108 pairs, the mean of individual follow-up-minus-baseline differences equals the follow-up mean minus the baseline mean calculated on those same pairs. It need not equal the difference between the means calculated from all 112 follow-up and all 114 baseline values.
This identity depends on using the same matched participants. It explains why matching and missingness checks precede a paired test. The numerical illustration in the paired-comparison chapter is a different teaching case with 30 complete pairs.

title: 6  Preparing Data for a Specific Analysis
section: 6.9 Confirm categorical denominators and event coding
text:
6.9 Confirm categorical denominators and event coding
For an event proportion, state the observation period, event definition, eligible population, and number with known status. Unknown status cannot be combined with confirmed absence merely to complete a two-by-two table.
In another invented illustration, 192 participants are eligible, 180 have known status, and 36 of these have the event. The observed-status proportion is 36/180=20\%. Dividing 36 by 192 gives 18.75%, but that calculation treats the 12 unknown statuses as contributing no recorded events to the full denominator.
Without additional information, between 36 and 48 of the 192 could have the event if every unknown status is respectively absent or present. The corresponding 18.75% to 25% range is a simple accounting bound. It is not a confidence interval and does not resolve the missingness mechanism.
Report the known-status calculation with its denominator and missing count. If a full eligible-population quantity is intended, justify how unknown outcomes are handled. The design also matters: case-control sampling does not generally allow the sampled event fraction to be interpreted as population risk.
For a binary model, verify which category is the event and which predictor level is the reference. The labels 0 and 1 need an explicit dictionary. A change in coding can reverse an odds-ratio comparison without changing the underlying records.

title: 6  Preparing Data for a Specific Analysis
section: 6.10 Prepare assumption checks without automatic test switching
text:
6.10 Prepare assumption checks without automatic test switching
Inspect appropriate summaries and graphs for the chosen question. Independent group comparisons need group distributions and counts. Paired inference needs within-pair differences. Regression needs the relationship and relevant residual patterns. Categorical procedures need the observed table and, for an approximation, attention to expected counts.
A preliminary test result should not operate as an automatic switch between methods that target different quantities. A significant normality test does not by itself establish that a mean is no longer the research target. A non-significant test does not prove that the relevant model is adequate.
Resolve data errors first. Then evaluate whether the method is suitable, whether an alternative preserves or changes the target quantity, and whether the available sample supports the intended inference. Document that reasoning in the analysis record.

title: 6  Preparing Data for a Specific Analysis
text:
6.11 Keep the analytical record reproducible
Save the reviewed source version, dictionary, cleaning log, derivation definitions, eligibility rules, required-variable list, method settings, and analytical sample counts. The saved jamovi analysis should be identifiable as belonging to that record, with software and module versions documented when relevant.
A CSV export can carry values without carrying the full set of analysis settings and transformation definitions. Retain the saved analysis file as well as a suitable data export when both are needed for review. Confirm what survives each export rather than assuming that every format preserves the same information.
Reopen the saved file and verify that the intended variables, filters, counts, and results remain available. If an updated source is imported, repeat the count and derivation checks. A refreshed file may produce different results even when the analytical options have not changed.

section: 6.12 Report the final sample and decisions
text:
6.12 Report the final sample and decisions
Describe the eligible population, required measurements, missing-data handling, and method. Give group counts or complete-pair counts where relevant. Explain exclusions using their actual reasons rather than a single unexplained phrase such as “incomplete data were removed.”
For the complete-pair teaching example, a defensible methods statement is: “The paired analysis required both baseline and follow-up measurements. Of 120 eligible participants, 108 had a complete pair; six lacked baseline, eight lacked follow-up, and two lacked both. Change was defined as follow-up minus baseline.”
The result should then use those 108 pairs and acknowledge what incomplete follow-up means for the interpretation. Do not borrow an estimate from a different sample or the separate 30-pair illustration to complete the paragraph.

title: Descriptive Statistics and Graphs
text:
Description answers what was observed: how many participants were analysed, how variables were distributed, which values were missing, and how groups differed in their observed characteristics. A descriptive table should therefore identify the denominator and measurement unit, not merely display numbers.
The next two chapters address numerical summaries and graphical presentation. Use both. A mean and standard deviation can conceal skewness, multiple peaks, or an influential observation. A graph can reveal those features but may not communicate the exact count or estimate needed for reporting. The NIST handbook describes these complementary numerical and graphical approaches to exploratory analysis. [1, 2]
Describe the data before comparing groups. This order helps identify coding problems and clarifies which statistical quantity would answer the question. A choice between a mean and a median should reflect the objective and distribution, rather than a rule that every variable must be reduced to the same summary.
By the end of this part, the reader should be able to construct a descriptive table, select a suitable graph, and explain the important features of an observed distribution.
