2. NIST/SEMATECH. Measures of scale. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda356.htm [accessed 5 Oct. 2026].

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text: 7.1 Learning objectives

7.1 Learning objectives
After this chapter, the reader should be able to report counts with denominators, select appropriate measures of central value and spread, distinguish standard deviation from standard error, and interpret a descriptive estimate with its uncertainty.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text: After this chapter, the reader should be able to report counts with denominators, select appropriate measures of central value and spread, distinguish standard deviation from standard error, and interpret a descriptive estimate with its uncertainty.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text:
7.2 Describe the observed sample first
Start with the number of eligible observations, the number included in the analysis, and the availability of key variables. Then describe variables using summaries that retain their meaning and units. Description is a check on the data and a basis for later method selection.
Suppose 200 participants are enrolled and 180 provide a follow-up measurement. The enrolled sample and the observed follow-up sample are different denominators. A report should state which denominator is used for each summary, rather than placing 200 at the top of every table column.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text:
7.3 Frequencies, proportions, and percentages
A frequency is a count. A proportion divides a count by a defined denominator. A percentage multiplies a proportion by 100. In an invented example, 40 participants with an event among 200 participants with known event status gives

\hat p=\frac{40}{200}=0.20=20\%.

Write “40 of 200 participants (20.0%)” rather than “20%” alone. The count and denominator indicate how much information supports the proportion. The same percentage based on 5 observations and 5,000 observations has very different estimation precision.
Distinguish percentages of all eligible participants from percentages among those with an observed value. If 40 events are recorded among 180 participants with known status and 20 statuses are unknown, the observed proportion is 40/180, or 22.2%. Reporting 40/200 would require an explicit assumption about the unknown statuses; it is not a neutral alternative.

7.3.1 Row and column percentages
In a table comparing event status by group, a row percentage can answer “What fraction of group A had an event?” A column percentage can answer “What fraction of participants with an event belonged to group A?” These are different conditional descriptions. State the denominator in the table title or note.
jamovi’s contingency-table analysis can display observed counts and row, column, or total percentages. Select the percentage that answers the question and check the orientation of the table. [1]

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text:
7.4 Mean, median, and mode
The arithmetic mean is the sum of values divided by their number. The median is the middle ordered value, using the mean of the two middle values when the sample size is even. The mode identifies the most frequent value or category. These summaries describe different aspects of a distribution. [2]
Consider invented waiting times, in minutes:

2,\ 3,\ 3,\ 4,\ 4,\ 5,\ 6,\ 7,\ 8,\ 18.

The sum is 60, so the mean is 6.0 minutes. The middle values are 4 and 5, so the median is 4.5 minutes. The long wait of 18 minutes pulls the mean upward. Neither result is a calculation error; they answer different descriptive questions about the same observations.
If the concern is a typical person’s waiting experience, the median and spread of the central values may be helpful. If the concern is total waiting time divided by the number of attendees, the mean has a direct role. Select the summary according to the question and show enough of the distribution to avoid concealing the long waits.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
section: 7.5 Standard deviation, variance, range, and IQR
text:
7.5 Standard deviation, variance, range, and IQR
The sample standard deviation describes dispersion around the mean and retains the original measurement unit. Variance is its square. The range spans the minimum and maximum. The interquartile range is the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile and describes the width of the middle half of the distribution. [3]
For the waiting-time example, the sample SD is 4.62 minutes. The minimum is 2 and the maximum is 18 minutes. Using the interpolation convention in the accompanying verification script, the first and third quartiles are 3.25 and 6.75 minutes, giving an IQR of 3.50 minutes.
Quartile algorithms can give different values in a small sample; report the method when exact reproduction matters. R documents several quantile definitions, with type 7 used by default in its quantile() function. [4]
When writing a median summary, give the two quartile limits rather than an ambiguous single “IQR” number if readers need to see the central interval: “median 4.5 minutes, first–third quartile 3.25–6.75.” For a mean summary, write “mean 6.0 minutes (SD 4.6).” Preserve the distinction between a measure of location and a measure of spread.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
section: 7.6 Standard deviation is not standard error
text:
7.6 Standard deviation is not standard error
The SD describes variation among individual observations. The SE describes the sampling variability of an estimate. For a mean of independent observations, the estimated SE is

SE(\bar x)=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.

The SD and sample size determine the standard error used in the conventional confidence interval for a mean. [5]
In an invented sample with SD 18 mmHg and 100 observations, the SE of the mean is 1.8 mmHg. This does not mean that individual blood pressures differ from the mean by only 1.8 mmHg. The smaller number describes uncertainty about the estimated mean, not the variation among people.
Increasing sample size can reduce the SE while the observed individual variation remains similar. When the purpose is to describe participants, report the SD. When the purpose is to estimate a population mean, report the mean with an appropriate confidence interval.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text:
7.7 Confidence intervals for descriptive estimates
A confidence interval adds an uncertainty summary to a point estimate. For a mean, a conventional interval uses the estimated SE and a t-distribution critical value under its assumptions. For a proportion, several interval methods exist, and the method should be identified rather than assumed from the percentage alone. An exact binomial interval is one documented option. [6]
For an invented mean of 136 mmHg, SD 18 mmHg, and 100 independent observations, the conventional two-sided 95% t interval is 132.43 to 139.57 mmHg. This example concerns uncertainty in the mean. It is not an interval describing where 95% of individual blood pressure values lie.
Interpret confidence as a property of the interval-generating procedure under its assumptions. In repeated sampling, a 95% procedure covers the population parameter in approximately 95% of repetitions. It is not a frequentist probability of 95% that the fixed parameter lies within this particular realised interval. The next chapter develops this interpretation in more detail. [5]

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text:
7.9 Describe groups without overinterpreting them
Group-specific summaries show the observed distributions and denominators. They do not alone establish whether an intervention caused a difference or whether a population contrast is estimated precisely. Those judgments require the design and inferential method.
For an illustrative table, display the group label, number with an observed value, mean with SD or median with quartile limits, and measurement unit. Use the same summary convention across groups unless a difference is explained. Describe missing values separately instead of embedding them in the denominator silently.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text:
7.10 Reporting example

For the invented waiting times: “Waiting time was available for 10 observations. The median was 4.5 minutes (first–third quartile 3.25–6.75), with values ranging from 2 to 18 minutes. The mean was 6.0 minutes (SD 4.6), reflecting the influence of the longest wait.”

This statement gives the availability, location, spread, unit, and reason for displaying both mean and median. A report would usually choose the summaries most relevant to its objective rather than repeat all available numbers.

title: 7  Descriptive Statistics
text:
7.11 Common errors
Avoid giving percentages without denominators, using SEM to describe individual variation, averaging category codes, reporting identical denominators despite variable-specific missingness, or treating a confidence interval for the mean as the range of individual measurements. Check that each number has the intended role before interpreting it.

section: 8.2 Let the question determine the graph
text:
8.2 Let the question determine the graph
A graph should make one analytical task easier. A bar chart compares counts or proportions across categories. A histogram describes the distribution of a quantitative measurement. A scatterplot examines the relationship between two quantitative variables. A point with an interval displays an estimate and its uncertainty.
Before creating a graph, state what the reader should be able to see. “Compare the event proportions across groups” is a clearer task than “make a chart of the dataset.” The first task determines the denominator, category labels, and axis scale; the second leaves those decisions unresolved.

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.3 Bar charts for categories
Use separate bars for categories and label the axis as a count or percentage. Absolute count bars should start at zero so that their lengths correspond to the values. If percentages are shown, state whether they use the total sample, a group denominator, or only observations with known status.
For nominal categories, ordering may follow a meaningful convention or the magnitude of the count. For ordinal categories, preserve the order of the scale. Sorting mild, moderate, and severe by frequency would make the display harder to interpret as an ordered severity distribution.
Avoid three-dimensional effects and decorative shapes that make lengths difficult to compare. A pie chart can show a coarse part-to-whole division with a few exclusive categories, but a bar chart usually makes precise comparisons easier. If category membership overlaps, the displayed percentages should not be presented as parts of one exclusive whole.

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.4 Histograms for numerical distributions
A histogram divides a numerical axis into intervals and counts observations within them. It can show location, spread, asymmetry, multiple peaks, and potential unusual observations. The width of the intervals affects the apparent shape, so interpretation should not depend on one arbitrary choice of bins. [1]
Unlike a categorical bar chart, neighbouring histogram bins represent adjacent numerical intervals. The horizontal axis therefore retains a quantitative scale. Label the vertical axis accurately: frequency, relative frequency, or density are different representations and should not be used interchangeably.
The invented waiting times from the descriptive chapter illustrate a long upper tail. Most values are between 2 and 8 minutes, with one value of 18 minutes. The histogram shows where values are concentrated; the boxplot shows the central interval and the separated high observation.






Figure 8.1: Histogram and boxplot of the ten invented waiting times. Both panels use the same measurements; they emphasise different distributional features.



A second peak may represent a mixture of groups, a change in measurement procedures, or a feature of the underlying distribution. Inspect relevant grouping and timing variables before treating the pooled distribution as one homogeneous sample.

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.5 Boxplots and individual points
A boxplot usually displays the median and first–third quartile interval. A common fenced version uses whiskers extending to the most extreme observations within 1.5 IQR of the quartiles and displays observations beyond those limits separately. The whisker convention must be understood because it can differ across implementations. [2]
An observation beyond a whisker is flagged by a plotting rule; the graph has not established that it is erroneous. Verify the source and examine its relevance to the question. A valid high value may be an important part of the distribution.
For small groups, displaying individual observations alongside a boxplot can make the amount of data visible. A boxplot alone may hide whether a group has five observations or fifty. Show the group sample sizes and use a consistent scale across panels when comparing magnitudes.

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.6 Q–Q plots and distributional assumptions
A normal Q–Q plot compares the ordered observed values with values expected under a normal reference distribution. Approximate alignment with a straight line supports a normal approximation; systematic bends or tail departures identify features needing further assessment. In a regression, the relevant plot is typically for residuals rather than for every raw predictor. [3]
A Q–Q plot does not replace the design assumptions. Perfectly aligned observations can still come from repeated measurements treated incorrectly as independent. Conversely, a small tail departure does not by itself identify the best alternative analysis. Interpret the plot alongside sample size, unusual observations, and the target quantity.

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.7 Scatterplots before correlation
Plot one point per defined observation unit with the two variables on numerical axes. Inspect direction, form, spread, unusual points, and possible subgroups. A straight upward pattern suggests a positive linear relationship. A steadily increasing curve is monotonic but not necessarily linear. A U-shaped pattern can contain a strong relationship even when its linear correlation is close to zero.






Figure 8.2: Three invented coordinate examples distinguish a roughly linear relationship, a monotonic curve, and a U-shaped relationship. The axes are arbitrary numerical units; panels use separate vertical scales to compare their form.



Do not draw connecting lines between unrelated individuals. Lines imply an order or a relationship between adjacent points. Use a line only when the connection represents something defined, such as repeated measurements from one participant or an ordered time series.
The correlation chapter develops the distinction between Pearson’s linear coefficient and Spearman’s rank-based coefficient. The scatterplot provides the context in which those numbers should be read. [4]

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.8 Paired measurements and time
For two measurements from the same participant, connecting that participant’s two values preserves the matching. A plot of change values can then show whether changes are consistently in one direction or whether a few participants account for most of the mean change.
If follow-up times differ, state the time definition and window. A line from baseline to a common follow-up label should not conceal that observations were taken at substantially different times. More extensive longitudinal patterns require a design and analysis that account for their repeated structure.

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.9 Display uncertainty explicitly
An interval around a mean may describe a confidence interval, one standard deviation, a standard error, or a prediction interval. These have different meanings. State the interval type and level in the caption; a label of “error bars” alone is insufficient.
A CI for a mean describes estimation uncertainty. An SD describes individual spread. A prediction interval concerns a new observation under its model. A narrow CI therefore does not imply that individual values are tightly clustered. Similarly, overlap between two separate group intervals is not a direct test of the difference between those groups.
When the research question concerns a contrast, display the contrast itself with its interval and a relevant reference value. For a mean difference, the no-difference value is zero; for a ratio, the null value is one. Explain the chosen direction and scale in the caption.

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.10 Build a self-contained caption
A useful caption identifies the population or illustrative context, outcome and unit, groups or time points, sample size, and meaning of plotted summaries. If a graph shows invented teaching values, label them as invented. If a scale is transformed, state the transformation.
For example: “Distribution of invented waiting times for 10 observations. The histogram uses two-minute bins. The box shows the median and first–third quartiles; whiskers follow the 1.5-IQR convention. Points beyond the whiskers are plotted individually.”
The ICMJE guidance describes figures as part of the scientific report and requires units and legends that allow their meaning to be assessed. Apply that principle to a teaching figure as well as to a manuscript figure. [5]

title: 8  Graphical Presentation
text:
8.11 Common errors
Avoid missing denominators, unexplained axis truncation, different units across comparable panels, decorative three-dimensional bars, lines joining unrelated observations, and uncertainty intervals without a definition. Check the graph at its final printed size; a readable analysis window can become unreadable when reduced to a book page.

title: Core Inferential Methods
text:
Inference uses observed data to learn about a quantity beyond the sample. Its validity depends on the study design and analysis assumptions. Increasing sample size can reduce sampling uncertainty, but it does not by itself remove a systematic error in how participants were selected or measurements were obtained.
This part begins with estimates, confidence intervals, p-values, errors, and power. It then considers continuous outcomes in two or more groups and associations between categorical variables. Throughout, define the target quantity before selecting the test: a mean difference, a distributional comparison, a proportion, or a ratio.
The p-value and confidence interval provide different information. The p-value refers to the incompatibility of the observed data with a specified null model. The interval communicates estimation uncertainty under its assumptions. Neither replaces the magnitude of the estimate or the clinical question. [1, 2]
By the end of this part, the reader should be able to choose a basic independent or paired comparison, check the relevant assumptions, interpret uncertainty, and avoid treating a non-significant result as proof that two groups are equivalent.

text: 9.1 Learning objectives

9.1 Learning objectives

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text: After this chapter, the reader should be able to define a null hypothesis on the correct scale; explain a p-value and confidence interval; distinguish statistical from clinical importance; interpret Type I and Type II errors; and recognise why a non-significant result does not establish equivalence.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.2 Begin with an estimate
Suppose the question is whether mean follow-up blood pressure differs between groups A and B. The target quantity is the population mean in A minus the population mean in B. The sample provides an estimate of that quantity. A statistical analysis should report the estimate and its uncertainty even when it also conducts a hypothesis test.
The null value depends on the scale. A difference of zero represents no difference; a ratio of one represents equal quantities. Testing an odds ratio against zero would therefore be a scale error. Specify the estimand, group direction, and null value before interpreting the output.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
section: 9.3 Sampling distributions and the normal model
text:
9.3 Sampling distributions and the normal model
A sampling distribution describes how an estimator varies across repeated samples. It is different from the distribution of individual measurements in one sample. A normal distribution is symmetric and is described by a mean and standard deviation; the standard normal has mean zero and SD one. [1]
Under appropriate conditions, including independent, identically distributed sampling and finite positive variance in the basic version, the central limit theorem makes the distribution of a properly standardised sample mean approach a normal distribution as sample size increases. This does not require the individual measurements themselves to become normal. There is no universal sample-size cutoff that removes all problems from heavy tails, dependence, or influential observations. [2]
The t-based intervals introduced here account for estimating the unknown variance under the conventional model. Always connect the reference distribution to the statistic and assumptions rather than treating “normality” as a label applied to an entire dataset.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.4 Null and alternative hypotheses
The null hypothesis is the specified value or relationship being evaluated by a test. For a two-group mean comparison,

H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0.

A two-sided alternative is

H_1:\mu_A-\mu_B\ne0.

The model includes more than this equation: it also contains assumptions about the observations and their distribution. A p-value must be interpreted in relation to that model, not as a free-standing measure of truth.
A one-sided alternative addresses a prespecified direction. It should be justified by the question before the results are examined. Switching to a one-sided test after observing the direction of a difference changes the analysis procedure and its error properties.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.5 What a p-value means
A p-value is the probability, under the specified null model, of a test statistic at least as incompatible with that model as the observed statistic, according to the chosen test. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, the probability that the results arose “by chance,” or the magnitude of the effect. [3]
The conditioning is essential: the calculation begins by assuming the null model and evaluating the observed statistic within it. It does not assign a probability to the model itself. A small value identifies incompatibility with the null model but does not identify which assumption or feature accounts for that incompatibility.
Read the p-value alongside the estimate, CI, sample size, design, and analysis decisions. An extremely small difference can produce a small p-value in a large sample. A substantial estimate can have a large p-value when the data provide little precision. Neither situation is resolved by the threshold alone.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.6 Confidence intervals and sampling uncertainty
A confidence interval is produced by a procedure intended to cover a population parameter at a stated rate under its assumptions. In repeated sampling, a 95% procedure covers the parameter in approximately 95% of repetitions. Once one interval is observed, the fixed parameter is either inside or outside it; the confidence level is not a frequentist probability assigned to that particular inclusion. [4]
The interval can be read as a range of parameter values compatible with the observed data and model according to the interval procedure. This interpretation remains conditional on the design and analysis assumptions. It does not incorporate every possible bias or guarantee that values just outside the limits are impossible.






Figure 9.1: Repeated-sampling illustration of confidence intervals for a known mean. Each line is calculated from an invented simulated sample, and the vertical reference is the generating mean.



The figure demonstrates coverage across repetitions. It does not show 30 plausible positions for the same observed interval, and it is not a clinical dataset. Individual simulations need not yield exactly 95% coverage in a finite set of repetitions.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.7 Precision and clinical importance
Precision concerns the uncertainty of an estimate. Clinical importance concerns whether its magnitude matters for the stated clinical or research objective. Establish the relevant threshold or interpretation using subject knowledge and appropriate sources before drawing a conclusion. A teaching threshold should be labelled as illustrative.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
section: 9.8 Type I and Type II errors
text:
9.8 Type I and Type II errors
A Type I error is rejection of a true null hypothesis under the test procedure. The significance level, alpha, sets its nominal control under the relevant assumptions. A Type II error is failure to reject the null when a specified alternative is true. Power is one minus the Type II error probability for that alternative. [5]
Power is not a property of a sample size alone. It depends on the specified effect, variability, analysis, significance level, and other design features. A study can have good power for a large effect and poor power for a smaller effect. Define the effect that matters before calculating the required sample size. R’s power calculation documentation makes these inputs explicit for t-tests. [6]
Do not interpret alpha as the probability that a particular positive result is false. That statement conditions on a different event and requires additional information. Similarly, planned power is not the probability that one non-significant result is a false negative. The probability definitions concern repetitions of a specified procedure and model.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.9 Non-significance and equivalence
When a test does not reject the null, the data may be compatible with zero and with a range of non-zero values. The CI indicates how broad that range is. A statement of “no difference” is especially misleading when the interval includes differences that would matter for the study objective. [7]
Equivalence and non-inferiority require their own prespecified margins, hypotheses, and analyses. A conventional superiority test with p greater than 0.05 does not answer those questions. In this volume, report the estimated difference and interval, then explain whether the remaining uncertainty includes relevant effects.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.10 Multiple analyses and selective interpretation
If many outcomes or subgroup comparisons are tested, the opportunity to obtain a small p-value somewhere increases. Define the primary question and distinguish prespecified analyses from exploration. Where multiple comparisons belong to one inferential family, select and report a suitable adjustment strategy. [8]
Adjusting p-values does not repair selective reporting of only the most favourable analysis. Report the relevant analysis family and explain which conclusions are confirmatory and which are exploratory. A change in method after seeing the result should be documented with its reason.

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.11 Assumptions belong to the interpretation
Every test is attached to an observation structure and a statistical model. Independence, pairing, category definitions, and measurement units should be checked before examining distributional assumptions. A normality check cannot establish that repeated observations are independent.
A diagnostic test’s non-significant result does not prove that its null hypothesis is true. Use plots, design information, and the sensitivity of the intended analysis to departures, rather than choosing methods solely by whether a preliminary p-value falls above or below 0.05. [9]

title: 9  Estimation and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9.12 Reporting an inferential result
A clear statement identifies the comparison and analytical sample, gives the estimate with units, reports the CI and method, and includes the test result when it is relevant. Its interpretation should remain proportionate to the design and uncertainty.
For the calculated teaching contrast: “Mean follow-up systolic blood pressure was 6.0 mmHg lower in group A than in group B (A minus B: −6.0 mmHg; 95% CI −11.4 to −0.6; Welch’s two-sided p = 0.031). The interval allows effects smaller and larger than the illustrative 5-mmHg threshold, so the estimate does not establish that the reduction is at least 5 mmHg.”

10.3 Decide what should be compared
A comparison of means targets an arithmetic difference. A rank-based comparison asks about the ordering or distribution of observations under its assumptions. A non-parametric test is not simply a mean test with the normality requirement removed.
Specify which quantity matters. If the objective concerns average resource use, a mean may remain relevant even when the distribution is skewed. If it concerns an ordered outcome or a distributional shift, a rank-based approach may be suitable. The choice should retain the original research objective.

title: 10  Comparing Two Groups or Two Paired Measurements
text:
10.4 Independent-samples t-tests

10.4.1 Welch’s method
Welch’s t-test estimates a mean difference using the two sample variances separately. It does not impose the equal-variance assumption of the pooled Student method. R documents the Welch/Satterthwaite degrees-of-freedom calculation and distinguishes it from the pooled-variance option. [1]
For groups A and B,

\widehat\Delta=\bar x_A-\bar x_B,
\qquad
SE(\widehat\Delta)=\sqrt{\frac{s_A^2}{n_A}+\frac{s_B^2}{n_B}}.

The test compares this difference with the specified null value using the appropriate t reference distribution. A confidence interval adds and subtracts the relevant critical value multiplied by the SE.
Welch’s method addresses unequal variances; it does not repair dependence, invalid coding, or an outcome dominated by a few influential observations. Inspect those issues separately. In small samples, major departures from the intended distributional model require particular attention.


10.4.2 Pooled Student’s method
The pooled independent t-test uses a shared variance estimate. Its interpretation requires a defensible equal-variance model in addition to the independent-observation and distributional conditions. A preliminary variance test alone should not determine whether those assumptions are scientifically reasonable.
If the pooled method is used, explain why the common-variance model is appropriate. If Welch’s method is used, report it by name rather than labelling every independent comparison simply as “a t-test.” The choice affects the SE and degrees of freedom when group variances or sizes differ.


10.4.3 Check the data before reading the test
Confirm the group labels, outcome unit, group counts, missingness, and contrast direction. Inspect each group’s distribution and check verified extreme values for their influence. Distinguish a coding error from a genuine unusual observation. The analysis should follow the specified estimand rather than change because one version gives a smaller p-value.

text:
10.6 Paired t-test
The paired t-test analyses the within-pair differences. Define the direction, such as follow-up minus baseline, calculate a difference for each complete pair, and estimate the mean difference with its SE. The distributional assumption used for the conventional small-sample t inference concerns the differences, not separate normality tests for the two measurement columns. [3]
For differences d_i,

\bar d=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_i,
\qquad SE(\bar d)=\frac{s_d}{\sqrt n}.

The model requires independence between the pairs for this simple analysis. It does not require independence between the two measurements within each pair; that dependence is why the pairing is retained.
Confirm matching by identifier rather than row order alone when measurements were imported from separate files. Excluding a participant with one missing measurement changes the complete-pair sample. Report how many pairs are available and examine whether incomplete follow-up limits the interpretation.

10.6.1 Calculated paired illustration

In an invented example of 30 complete pairs, the mean baseline value is 146 mmHg and the mean follow-up value is 138 mmHg. The mean difference, follow-up minus baseline, is −8.0 mmHg, and the SD of the differences is 10.0 mmHg.

The paired SE is 10/\sqrt{30}=1.826 mmHg. The t statistic is −4.382 with 29 degrees of freedom. The 95% CI for mean change is −11.73 to −4.27 mmHg, and the two-sided p-value is 0.000141. Report p < 0.001 at an appropriate precision.
The estimate describes average within-participant change. A before–after study without an appropriate comparison does not isolate the reason for that change. Time trends, additional care, regression to the mean, and incomplete follow-up may remain relevant. The statistical result should not be labelled a treatment effect solely because the change is non-zero.

text:
10.7 Mann–Whitney U test
The Mann–Whitney test uses the relative ranks of observations in two independent groups. It is useful for an ordered or distributional comparison under its assumptions. An interpretation as a simple location or median shift requires additional conditions, such as comparable distributional shapes; it is not automatically a test of two medians. [5]
For a small invented illustration, let A contain 2, 4, 6, and 8, and B contain 1, 3, 5, and 7. The combined ranks for A are 2, 4, 6, and 8, with rank sum 20. Subtracting 4(4+1)/2=10 gives one convention for U_A=10.
Among the 16 A–B pairs, A is higher in 10, so the observed probability-of-superiority summary is 10/16 = 0.625, with no ties. This calculation helps explain the ordering information. It does not replace a test or interval appropriate to the chosen estimand, and the sample is too small for a precise population conclusion.
Software may report a rank-sum statistic or a transformed U statistic. Identify the definition when reproducing output. Ties and exact versus asymptotic calculations can also affect the reported p-value, so record the selected approach.

title: 10  Comparing Two Groups or Two Paired Measurements
text:
10.8 Wilcoxon signed-rank test
The signed-rank test is for paired differences or a one-sample difference distribution. It ranks the non-zero absolute differences and uses their signs. Its conventional location interpretation assumes a suitably symmetric difference distribution; it is not an assumption-free alternative for any paired dataset. [5]
For invented differences −4, −2, −1, 3, and 6, the ranks of the absolute differences are 4, 2, 1, 3, and 5. The positive rank sum is 3 + 5 = 8, and the negative rank sum is 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. This example shows why the signed-rank method uses both direction and ranked magnitude, rather than just counting positive changes.
If a difference distribution is strongly asymmetric, consider whether a different estimand or method is required. The paired t-test targets a mean change; the signed-rank procedure targets a different distributional feature. Changing tests should not be described as preserving the same question automatically.

Retain the effect on its original scale when that scale is clinically interpretable. A −6-mmHg difference communicates more directly than a standardised label alone. A reporting sentence for the independent illustration is: “Group A had a lower mean follow-up systolic blood pressure than group B (128.0 versus 134.0 mmHg; n = 60 in each group). The mean difference, A minus B, was −6.0 mmHg (95% CI −11.4 to −0.6; Welch t = −2.19, df = 115.96, p = 0.031).”
For the paired illustration: “Among 30 complete pairs, mean follow-up minus baseline systolic blood pressure was −8.0 mmHg (SD of differences 10.0; 95% CI −11.7 to −4.3; paired t = −4.38, df = 29, p < 0.001).” The interpretation should then state the design limitations relevant to attributing the change.

title: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups
text:
11.2 Define groups, outcomes, and independence
Consider mean follow-up blood pressure across three independent groups. The outcome is continuous and the grouping variable has three levels. A one-way analysis considers one grouping factor. The number of groups does not change the need to define eligibility, units, missingness, and the observation structure.
Three measurements from the same participant are not three independent groups. Similarly, participants within shared facilities can have a clustered structure. These designs require an analysis that recognises their dependence, rather than an independent one-way ANOVA applied to every row.
Identify whether the objective is an overall assessment of group means or a particular comparison, such as intervention A versus a control. An overall test and a specific contrast answer different questions. Define the contrast when it is the primary scientific objective.
crumbs: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups

title: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups
text:
11.3 What a one-way ANOVA tests
The conventional one-way ANOVA evaluates the null hypothesis

H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k.

Its alternative is that the means are not all equal. A small omnibus p-value does not mean that every pair differs. It also does not identify the size or direction of any particular contrast.
The fixed-effects one-way model expresses an observation as a group-specific mean component plus an error. The conventional model assumes independent errors with a common variance and a normal distribution for the relevant inference. [1]
crumbs: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups

title: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups
section: 11.4 Why the procedure is called analysis of variance
text:
11.4 Why the procedure is called analysis of variance
ANOVA compares variation between group means with variation within groups. If the observed groups differ substantially relative to the variation among observations within groups, the resulting F statistic becomes larger under the comparison with the null model.
The total squared variation is divided into between-group and within-group components. Each is converted to a mean square by dividing by its degrees of freedom. For k independent groups and N observations,

F=\frac{MS_{\text{between}}}{MS_{\text{within}}},
\qquad df_1=k-1,\quad df_2=N-k.

The F value is a test statistic, not a measurement of a clinical difference. Retain group summaries and the relevant contrast estimates when reporting the result.
crumbs: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups

title: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups
text:
11.5 Assess the conventional assumptions
Independence is established by design and data structure. A plot cannot prove it. Inspect whether participants contribute once to the comparison and whether matching or clustering needs to be accounted for.
Distributional assessment concerns within-group deviations or model residuals, rather than the pooled outcome distribution alone. Three groups with different means can create a non-normal-looking pooled distribution even when the within-group model is reasonable. Examine the appropriate residual or group plots.
The conventional model also assumes a common variance. Consider the observed spreads, sample sizes, and sensitivity to departures. A non-significant preliminary variance test does not prove that the variances are equal. Choosing a method solely from that preliminary p-value is an incomplete decision rule.

title: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups
text:
11.6 Welch’s one-way ANOVA
Welch’s one-way procedure compares group means while relaxing the common-variance assumption. It uses group-specific variability and an adjusted reference distribution. R’s oneway.test() documentation distinguishes the Welch approach from the equal-variance method, and jamovi’s simplified One-Way ANOVA offers a Welch option. [2, 3]
Welch’s method does not resolve dependence or a poor match between the intended estimand and the observed outcome. A skewed distribution with a few highly influential values still requires assessment. Report the selected method and its numerator and denominator degrees of freedom as displayed, including non-integer values where appropriate.
Choose follow-up procedures consistent with the variance model. A method based on a pooled common variance should not be added automatically after selecting an unequal-variance analysis.

text:
11.8 Planned contrasts and post-hoc comparisons
A planned contrast is specified from the research objective before inspecting the results. For example, a study may compare the average of two intervention groups with a control. Its coefficients and uncertainty calculation should match that defined comparison.
Post-hoc pairwise comparisons assess particular pairs, often after an overall exploration. With three groups there are three distinct pairs; with four there are six. State which family of comparisons is being evaluated and which adjustment or simultaneous interval procedure is used.
Tukey’s procedure provides simultaneous intervals for pairwise mean differences under its model. Games–Howell is an unequal-variance pairwise approach available in jamovi’s One-Way ANOVA documentation. These methods serve different assumptions and should be selected consistently with the main analysis. [3, 4]
A scientifically planned contrast need not be treated as a question that exists only after a significant omnibus test. Explain the inferential plan and multiplicity control appropriate to that objective. Conversely, reporting only the favourable pair after many unreported comparisons is selective reporting.

title: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups
text:
11.9 Multiple comparisons and error control
An adjustment applies to a defined family of analyses. Bonferroni controls a familywise error rate by a simple correction; Holm is a sequential familywise procedure. False-discovery-rate methods address a different error criterion. The intended criterion and family should be stated. [5]
Do not describe an adjusted p-value without identifying what was adjusted. A correction across the three group pairs is different from one across several outcomes, subgroup comparisons, and time points. The analysis plan should define the relevant family rather than allow it to change to obtain a preferred result.
An adjustment also does not turn an exploratory analysis into a prespecified confirmatory one. Preserve that distinction in the interpretation.

title: 11  Comparing More Than Two Groups
text:
11.10 Kruskal–Wallis test
The Kruskal–Wallis procedure uses ranks for comparisons across independent groups. It is appropriate for a defined rank-based or distributional question under its assumptions. Its location or median interpretation requires additional conditions about distributional shapes; it should not automatically be described as an ANOVA of medians. [6]
As with ANOVA, a global result does not identify which groups differ. Follow-up rank comparisons require a compatible method and a declared multiplicity approach. R documents pairwise Wilcoxon comparisons with p-value adjustment as one implementation route; the procedure chosen in jamovi should be identified by its actual name and version. [7, 8]
Inspect group distributions before using a pure location interpretation. If one group differs mainly in spread and another in location, a global rank result may reflect more than a difference in central values. Show medians and quartile limits as descriptions without claiming that these alone define the test’s null hypothesis.

Confirm the continuous outcome and grouping variable, then identify the conventional, Welch, or non-parametric procedure actually requested. Read group counts, summaries, diagnostic information, the overall statistic, and relevant contrast output. Check how missing observations were excluded. [3, 8]
When pairwise tables are present, verify the reference order of each difference, the CI or adjustment method, and the family to which the comparisons belong. Different contrast directions can coexist in one output table; a sign should never be interpreted without its labels.

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
section: 12.2 Start with the design and denominator
text:
12.2 Start with the design and denominator
Consider whether an event occurs more often in group A than in group B. For an independent comparison, each participant contributes one group assignment and one event status. The table describes two categorical variables observed on the same set of independent participants.
Before calculating a percentage, establish who was eligible to contribute to the event denominator and whether status is known. A recorded absence is different from an unknown outcome. If follow-up is incomplete, a simple event proportion may fail to answer the intended risk question.
The study design determines the interpretation. An event proportion over defined follow-up can describe risk when its denominator and ascertainment support that meaning. A cross-sectional proportion may describe prevalence. A rate uses an appropriate person-time denominator and is a different quantity. In a case-control sample, selection by outcome means the sampled case proportion is not the population risk.

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
text:
12.4 Pearson chi-square test of independence
The null model states that the two categorical variables are independent. It specifies expected cell counts calculated from the row and column totals:

E_{ij}=\frac{(\text{row total}_i)(\text{column total}_j)}{N}.

The test statistic summarises the observed deviations from these expected counts:

\chi^2=\sum_{i,j}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}},
\qquad df=(r-1)(c-1).

This is a test of association, not a measure of the magnitude of the association. R’s documentation describes the Pearson procedure, continuity correction for a 2-by-2 table, and a simulation-based option. [1]
In the invented table, the expected event count in each group is 22.5, and the expected absent count is 77.5. The uncorrected Pearson statistic is 6.452 with one degree of freedom, giving p = 0.0111. The estimate of association still needs to be reported separately.

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
text:
12.5 Expected counts and sparse tables
The adequacy of the chi-square approximation concerns expected counts, not simply observed counts or overall sample size. A large total sample can still contain sparse cells when one category is rare. Examine the table dimensions and the distribution of expected counts.
One commonly used screening convention checks for no expected count below one and a high proportion of expected counts at least five. R’s documented hybrid Fisher procedure uses more than 80% at least five and none below one. These are approximation rules within a defined procedure, not a universal guarantee of validity for every table. [2]
For a sparse 2-by-2 table, Fisher’s exact procedure is a common option. For larger tables, an appropriate exact or Monte Carlo procedure may be needed, subject to computational feasibility and software availability. State the method and, for simulations, the number of repetitions and relevant reproducibility settings.
Yates continuity correction applies to a 2-by-2 chi-square calculation. It is not a general repair for sparse tables of arbitrary dimensions. Select the procedure using observation structure, dimensions, expected counts, and the question rather than overall sample size alone. [1]
Do not combine categories merely to make a test run unless the grouping is substantively defensible. Category merging changes the question and should be documented.

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
text:
12.6 Fisher’s exact procedure
Fisher’s test evaluates the table conditional on its margins under the independence model. For the invented 2-by-2 table, the two-sided p-value is 0.0171. This differs from the uncorrected Pearson p-value because the procedures use different inferential calculations.
An “exact” calculation does not remove the need for appropriate observation structure or eliminate every uncertainty about design. The term identifies how the probability is calculated under the model. The two-sided definition and reported odds-ratio estimator can also vary by procedure; R’s Fisher documentation uses a conditional estimate rather than the simple cross-product ratio. [2]
When reporting, identify the chosen procedure rather than selecting whichever p-value is smaller. The point estimate and interval should also be labelled with their calculation method.

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
text:
12.7 Risk or prevalence difference
Under the stated teaching follow-up, the risk difference is

RD=\frac{30}{100}-\frac{15}{100}=0.15.

This is 15 percentage points, not a 15% relative increase. Its large-sample Wald 95% CI in this illustration is approximately 3.6 to 26.4 percentage points. The absolute difference communicates how much the group-specific proportions differ on the original probability scale.
If the same table arose from a cross-sectional study, use an interpretation appropriate to prevalence rather than follow-up risk. If it arose from outcome-based sampling, do not calculate a population risk difference from the sampled case fractions.

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
text:
12.8 Risk ratio and odds ratio
For the teaching follow-up table,

RR=\frac{30/100}{15/100}=2.00.

The group A event risk is twice that in B under the stipulated design and complete follow-up. A log-scale large-sample 95% CI is 1.15 to 3.48.
Odds are probability divided by its complement. Group A odds are 30/70; group B odds are 15/85. The sample odds ratio is

OR=\frac{30/70}{15/85}=\frac{30\times85}{70\times15}=2.43.

Its log-Wald 95% CI is 1.21 to 4.87. The odds ratio and risk ratio differ because odds and probability differ. An OR of 2.43 here is not a statement that the event probability is 2.43 times as high. Bland and Altman’s Statistics Note explains the odds-ratio calculation and interpretation. [3]
The approximation of an OR to an RR depends on the outcome probabilities and context; it should not be assumed without checking. Always name the reported measure and reference category.

12.8.1 Interpret interval methods carefully
The Wald intervals above are teaching calculations appropriate to the stated positive cell counts and large-sample approximation. They are not presented as the exact intervals returned by Fisher’s procedure. With small or zero counts, the simple log formulas can fail or perform poorly, requiring a suitable alternative method.

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
text:
12.9 Larger contingency tables
For more than two rows or columns, the overall chi-square test evaluates independence across the complete table. Its result does not identify a particular category as the cause of the association. Examine observed counts, relevant percentages, and prespecified comparisons before drawing a category-specific conclusion.
Cramér’s V can summarise the strength of an association without giving its clinical direction. It is not a risk ratio, an odds ratio, or the proportion of participants with an event. Prefer question-specific contrasts when available and substantively useful.
jamovi’s contingency-table analysis can display observed and expected counts, percentages, test results, and several association measures. Select the quantities appropriate to the table and design; an available checkbox does not establish that every measure is meaningful for that study. [4]

title: 12  Associations Between Categorical Variables
text:
12.10 Paired binary outcomes: McNemar’s question
If the same participants have a binary status before and after an observation period, the data are paired. A 2-by-2 table now cross-classifies before and after status rather than two independent groups. McNemar’s procedure evaluates marginal symmetry and uses the discordant pairs for the comparison. [5]
In an invented table, suppose 20 participants have the event at both times, 15 change from present to absent, 5 change from absent to present, and 60 are absent at both times. There are 100 pairs, but only the 20 discordant pairs inform the change-direction comparison. The before proportion is 35% and the after proportion is 25%.
An independent Pearson test applied as if the before and after samples were unrelated would discard the pairing. Use a paired categorical procedure, with an exact conditional approach considered when the discordant counts require it. A binomial calculation on the discordant counts is one exact route under the paired null model. [6, 7]

text:
12.11 Reporting example

For the independent teaching illustration: “The event occurred in 30 of 100 participants in group A (30.0%) and 15 of 100 in B (15.0%). Under the stipulated common follow-up, the risk ratio for A versus B was 2.00 (log-Wald 95% CI 1.15–3.48), and the absolute risk difference was 15.0 percentage points (Wald 95% CI 3.6–26.4). The uncorrected Pearson chi-square test gave χ²(1) = 6.45, p = 0.011.”

This statement names the denominators, measures, directions, interval methods, and test. It does not describe the association as causal. If a different design or procedure is used, revise those elements rather than transplanting this wording unchanged.

title: Correlation and Introductory Regression
text:
Association asks whether two variables vary together. Regression goes further by specifying an outcome and describing how its expected value changes with a predictor. These methods require an explicit data structure and a clear interpretation of the analysis scale.
The correlation chapter distinguishes linear and monotonic relationships and explains why a scatterplot is needed before interpreting a coefficient. The linear regression chapter introduces a continuous outcome with one predictor, the meaning of a slope, and basic residual assessment. The logistic chapter introduces a binary outcome, odds, and the transformation between model coefficients and odds ratios.
The emphasis in this volume is interpretation of simple, unadjusted relationships. Multiple predictors, confounder selection, interaction, detailed model strategy, and predictive validation are reserved for later volumes. A fitted association should not be described as an independent or causal effect merely because it is obtained from a regression model.

13.2 Define the association question
Consider whether age and systolic blood pressure vary together among study participants. Each participant contributes one age–blood-pressure pair. Neither variable is automatically an outcome in the correlation calculation; the purpose is to summarise their relationship.

Look for direction, form, spread, influential observations, and subgroups. The graphical-presentation chapter shows examples of a roughly linear relationship, a monotonic curve, and a U-shaped relationship. A single coefficient cannot communicate all those features.
A pooled association can depend on differences between subgroups rather than on the relationship within them. Inspect groups relevant to the question before treating a pooled coefficient as the whole explanation. This inspection does not itself adjust for confounding; it reveals a feature that may require a different analysis.
When a verified unusual observation strongly affects the coefficient, show or describe that influence. Do not remove it solely to obtain a preferred value. If a sensitivity analysis is justified, report the rule and its interpretation.

Inspect groups relevant to the question before treating a pooled coefficient as the whole explanation. This inspection does not itself adjust for confounding; it reveals a feature that may require a different analysis.
When a verified unusual observation strongly affects the coefficient, show or describe that influence. Do not remove it solely to obtain a preferred value. If a sensitivity analysis is justified, report the rule and its interpretation.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.4 Pearson’s correlation coefficient
Pearson’s r describes linear association after scaling the covariance by the two standard deviations:

r=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}}.

It ranges from −1 to +1 when both variables have non-zero variation. A positive value indicates that larger values tend to occur together in a linear pattern; a negative value indicates the opposite direction. A constant variable does not provide the variation needed for this coefficient.
The coefficient is a descriptive calculation and does not require normality merely to exist. Its conventional small-sample test and interval use additional model assumptions. R documents the t-based Pearson test under independent observations from a suitable normal model and a Fisher-transformation interval. [1]

13.4.1 Direction and magnitude
The sign communicates direction. The absolute magnitude indicates how closely the observed values follow a linear relationship in their standardised scale. It does not indicate the slope in mmHg per year or the size of a clinical effect in original units.
Avoid using “weak,” “moderate,” or “strong” as universal clinical conclusions. Such labels are conventions, and their value depends on the measurement reliability, population range, and research objective. Report the numerical coefficient, uncertainty, sample size, and scatterplot context before adding any descriptive label.


13.4.2 Why zero does not mean no relationship
A near-zero Pearson coefficient can occur when positive and negative linear components balance in a curved pattern. In a symmetric U-shaped example, outcomes vary systematically with the predictor while the linear coefficient is zero. The graph is therefore necessary to distinguish lack of a linear association from lack of any relationship.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.5 Spearman’s rank correlation
Spearman’s coefficient applies correlation to the ranks of the paired values. It describes monotonic association: whether values tend to move in one direction together, without requiring a straight-line pattern in the original units. Ties need an appropriate ranking and inferential calculation. [1]
An increasing curve can have a high rank correlation even when its original-scale relationship is not linear. A U-shaped relationship is not generally monotonic over its full range, so substituting Spearman for Pearson does not automatically summarise every curve well.
Choose Spearman because ranks and monotonic ordering match the question and data. Do not describe it as a method that ignores all assumptions or repairs invalid observation matching. Independence between pairs remains relevant to the conventional inferential calculation.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.6 Inference for Pearson’s coefficient
For a conventional test of zero population correlation,

t=r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}},\qquad df=n-2.

The p-value refers to that null model. It is not the probability that the correlation is causal or that a future sample will show the same magnitude.
An approximate interval can be formed using Fisher’s transformation:

z=\operatorname{atanh}(r),\qquad SE(z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-3}},

then transforming the interval limits back with the hyperbolic tangent. This is an interval for Pearson’s population correlation under the method’s assumptions. Do not use it as an unlabelled interval for a different coefficient.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.7 Calculated illustration

Suppose an invented Pearson result is r=0.60 from 50 complete, independent pairs. The t statistic is approximately 5.20 with 48 degrees of freedom, giving a two-sided p-value of 0.00000412. The approximate Fisher 95% CI is 0.386 to 0.753.

The estimate indicates positive linear association, but the interval permits a range of magnitudes. It does not say that a one-year age increase changes blood pressure by 0.60 mmHg. That original-scale question requires a regression slope or another suitable model.
For comparison, an invented r=0.30 with the same 50 pairs has p = 0.0343 and a Fisher interval of approximately 0.024 to 0.534. A threshold label alone would hide the uncertainty in its magnitude. These are separate numerical teaching cases, not outcomes selected from one clinical dataset.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.8 Correlation is not causation
An association may reflect a causal pathway, a common cause, selection, measurement structure, or other features of the study. A correlation coefficient does not distinguish these explanations. The design and substantive knowledge determine which interpretation is defensible.
For example, a relationship between age and blood pressure does not specify what would happen if one could intervene on age, nor does it isolate the influence of other characteristics. Later volumes address adjustment and causal reasoning. This volume reports the observed relationship with an explicit boundary on interpretation.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.9 Correlation is not agreement
Two measurement methods can correlate perfectly while differing systematically. If method B equals method A plus 20 units for every observation, the linear correlation is +1, but the methods do not give the same values. A method-comparison question therefore requires assessment of differences and agreement, not correlation alone.
Reliability, agreement, and diagnostic accuracy have different targets. A high correlation does not establish that one method can replace another clinically. The relevant specialist methods are developed in later volumes.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.10 Correlation matrices and missingness
A matrix can present correlations among several variables. Inspect which observations contribute to each pair and whether the sample sizes differ. A coefficient based on 50 complete pairs and another based on 35 pairs do not have the same information, even if they appear in one matrix.
jamovi’s correlation analysis provides Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall options, sample-size display, and graphical and uncertainty options. Verify which outputs apply to the selected coefficient and record the method. [2]
If many correlations are examined, distinguish the prespecified relationship from exploratory screening. Multiplicity and selective interpretation remain relevant; a matrix of flagged p-values is not a model-selection strategy by itself.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.11 The relationship with simple regression
In an ordinary least-squares regression with one quantitative predictor, an intercept, and the same complete observations, R^2=r^2. This relationship does not make the two analyses interchangeable. Correlation is symmetric in the two variables, while regression specifies an outcome and produces a slope in defined units.
The regression chapter explains why those units, residuals, and prediction uncertainty matter. A numerical association summary should lead to a clearer question, not to an automatic causal explanation.

title: 13  Correlation
text:
13.12 Reporting example

For the invented 50-pair result: “Age and systolic blood pressure showed a positive linear association (Pearson r = 0.60; approximate Fisher 95% CI 0.39–0.75; n = 50; p < 0.001). Interpretation requires the scatterplot and the observation structure; the coefficient does not establish a causal effect or an original-scale increase per year.”

In a completed study report, describe the actual scatterplot assessment and any influential observations or design limitation. Avoid adding an unsupported strength category when the numerical result and context are more informative.

14.2 Specify the outcome and predictor
Suppose the question is how mean systolic blood pressure varies with age in the observed study population. Blood pressure is the outcome, and age is the predictor. Each independent participant contributes an outcome–predictor pair.

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
14.3 The simple linear model
The model expresses the outcome as

Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad E(\varepsilon_i\mid X_i)=0.

The intercept \beta_0 is the model’s conditional mean when X=0. The slope \beta_1 is the difference in conditional mean associated with a one-unit increase in X. The error represents the departure of an individual outcome from that conditional mean.
Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals. R’s lm() documentation identifies this as a route for fitting linear models and describes the model specification. [1]
The model is linear in its coefficients. The basic chapter uses a straight-line relationship with one predictor so that the slope’s units and interpretation are clear. More flexible relationships are developed later rather than forced into the same interpretation.

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
section: 14.4 Interpret the slope in its units
text:
14.4 Interpret the slope in its units
In a deliberately specified teaching equation,

\widehat{\text{SBP}}=100+0.50\times\text{age},

the slope is 0.50 mmHg per year. A ten-year age difference corresponds to a five-mmHg difference in the fitted conditional mean under this equation. It is an association in the specified model, not a claim that changing age causes blood pressure to change.
The fitted mean at age 40 is 120 mmHg; at age 50 it is 125 mmHg. These are values generated by the teaching equation, not predictions validated in a clinical population. Do not use them to guide care.
Scaling the predictor changes the numerical coefficient without changing the underlying fitted relationship. If age is expressed in decades, the same slope becomes 5.0 mmHg per decade. Always state the predictor unit.

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
section: 14.5 Interpret the intercept only where meaningful
text:
14.5 Interpret the intercept only where meaningful
The teaching equation gives an intercept of 100 mmHg at age zero. If the study includes adults only, age zero is outside the observed range. The intercept is part of the mathematical equation but may not have a useful substantive interpretation in that study.
Centering age at 40 would write the same fitted relationship as

\widehat{\text{SBP}}=120+0.50\times(\text{age}-40).

The intercept now describes the fitted mean at age 40, while the slope and fitted values are unchanged. This illustrates why a reference value can make an intercept easier to interpret.

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
14.6 Fitted values and residuals
A fitted value is the outcome value on the estimated mean line for a given predictor value. A residual is observed minus fitted:

e_i=y_i-\hat y_i.

If an invented participant aged 40 has observed SBP 132 mmHg, the teaching equation gives a fitted value of 120 and a residual of +12 mmHg. The residual indicates where that observation lies relative to the mean line; it is not a model coefficient.
Residual plots assess whether the mean relationship and error structure are suitable. Curvature, changing spread, and influential observations can identify aspects that a single fit summary conceals. NIST emphasises that a high R^2 does not establish adequate model fit. [2]






Figure 14.1: A correctly shaped linear teaching relationship has residuals without a systematic curve; fitting a straight line to a curved relationship leaves a visible residual pattern. All coordinates are invented for illustration.

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
section: 14.7 Assumptions and what they are needed for
text:
14.7 Assumptions and what they are needed for
The conditional mean should be represented adequately by the specified model. Observation or error dependence should be handled according to the study design. The conventional equal-variance SE assumes an appropriate constant error variance. Normality of errors supplies the conventional exact small-sample t inference, rather than a requirement that the raw predictor be normally distributed.
These conditions have different roles. It is possible to calculate an ordinary least-squares line without establishing that its usual confidence interval is valid. Examine the estimation and inference assumptions separately instead of treating “the regression ran” as confirmation of both.

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
section: 14.8 Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for the slope
text:
14.8 Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for the slope
A conventional slope interval has the form

\hat\beta_1\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\,SE(\hat\beta_1),

under the simple model’s assumptions. The corresponding null slope is zero. An interval excluding zero describes evidence of a non-zero linear association under that model; it does not establish a clinically important or causal effect.
For an invented summary with n = 60, slope 0.50 mmHg/year, and SE 0.10, the t statistic is 5.00 with 58 degrees of freedom. The 95% interval is approximately 0.30 to 0.70 mmHg/year. This summary is constructed for teaching; it is separate from the correlation example’s 50 observations.
Read the coefficient estimate and interval with its units. A standardised coefficient uses a different scale and should not be substituted silently for the original-scale slope.

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
text:
14.9 What R-squared describes
With an intercept, R^2 describes the proportion of the observed outcome sum of squared deviations accounted for by the fitted model. It is not the percentage of people correctly predicted or a guarantee that the model is useful in a new setting.
For the invented simple-model summary above, the corresponding R^2 is 25/(25+58)=0.301. This algebra follows from the simple regression test relationship. The remaining outcome variation is not made irrelevant by a non-zero slope.
A high R^2 can coexist with a poor functional form, influential observations, or invalid prediction outside the data. Check residuals and the intended use rather than selecting a model solely because this number is large. [2]

title: 14  Introduction to Simple Linear Regression
section: 14.10 Estimating a mean versus predicting an individual
text:
14.10 Estimating a mean versus predicting an individual
A confidence interval for the fitted conditional mean addresses uncertainty about the mean at a specified predictor value. A prediction interval for a new individual also includes the unexplained individual variation. Under the model, the latter is wider because it answers a different question. [3]
Do not use a narrow mean interval to suggest that individual outcomes can be predicted equally precisely. Similarly, an estimated mean relationship within the observed age range does not validate extrapolation to an age far outside that range.
Prediction-model development requires additional assessment of performance and validation. Those tasks are beyond this introductory association model and are reserved for later volumes.

text:
14.11 A binary predictor as a mean comparison
A predictor coded 0 for group B and 1 for A gives an intercept representing the mean in B and a slope representing A minus B in the simple unadjusted model. This links regression coefficients to the mean-difference question introduced earlier.
The usual pooled regression SE corresponds to its variance model. It should not be assumed to reproduce the unequal-variance Welch calculation merely because the coefficient estimate is the same. Preserve the intended inference assumptions as well as the estimand.

text: 15.1 Learning objectives

15.1 Learning objectives
